speechtext: Order.

We have in this, country a divided allegiance the fatal danger of which must have been brought home to every thoughtful man. No country can possess the peace and harmony necessary to stability whose people are not of one mind as to where the sovereign power resides. The fact is we have been trying to get along under two governments, the one at Ottawa and the other a self-constituted authority claiming the right to regulate federal and provincial legislation in regard to education. I have never meddled in my life with the doctrines, dogmas or ceremonies of any church. 1 have never had any desire to do so. I have never had any desire to interfere with any man in his right to worship as his conscience dictates. The last thing that would occur to me would be to interfere with him in the exercise of that right. But surely I am not guilty of intolerance when I assert that the Government should not favour one creed more than another.

Is that intolerance? Is it fanatical to say that public money should not be spent on sectarian education? Is it bigotry to assert that all citizens stand on the same level as regards privileges? Should I be charged with a desire to destroy religion because I believe that a system of national, nonsectarian schools will conduce to harmony and national unity?
We often hear it said that our differences in this country are due to misunderstanding. I dissent from that statement at once. I say our differences are not due to misunderstanding. We understand perfectly. It is because of the thorough understanding that we do have the differences that we have to-day. Do you mean to tell me that a man who resides in a certain section of the country and finds himself in the position that his children cannot attend the only school that there is for them because of certain religious dogmas being taught that he does not agree with, feels a sense of injustice because of misunderstanding? Not at all. He understands that he is not getting a square deal. There is not a man in this House who can argue successfully that he is getting a square deal. It is not a question of theology or of doctrine or religious dogma but it is a question of civil rights and a square deal for every man in this country.
Let me ask this question: Is a Government justified in conferring special privileges on any one section of the people? That is a fair question. If not, if you answer that in the negative, if you say that the Government is not justified in conferring special privileges on one section of the people, then you must agree with me that separate school laws are wrong in principle because they are a violation of the equality^ of civil rights which is the basis of free government.
What do I suggest in regard to this matter? I know that education in so far as Ontario and Quebec are concerned is fixed by the terms of Confederation. I do not wish to be understood as saying that I think this Parliament should take away from these provinces the rights which they have under the constitution. But surely that does not prevent us from discussing the question here as to whether another system would be preferable. We have had over fifty years of Confederation and the idea of the Fathers of Confederation was unquestionably in the main to try and unite the people.
I leave it to any hon. gentleman here who has studied past history and who reads

the press to say if he is satisfied with the conditions which exist in this country at the present time. After over fifty years of confederation have we got unity in this country? Not by any means. We have not got unity, and why have we not? Because, Mr. Speaker, we have had in the public life of this country in times past men who were willing to put party expediency and party exigencies before their duty to Canada; that is why. Because we have had in this country men calling themselves statesmen and posing as being especially broadminded who have been too cowardly to deal with questions such as this on their merits. That is why-at any rate it is my own opinion.
Now, Sir, I would suggest that this matter of education does concern the Federal Government and does concern this Parliament. Surely we have some interest in a democracy in Canada which is_ getting its ideas of Canada and of Britain, and of Canadian and British history, through the medium of half a dozen different foreign languages? Surely some right is vested in the Federal Government as to the, kind of democracy we are creating in this country? Is it not true that under existing conditions to-day we have less efficiency all over the country in regard to educational matters in our primary schools than we would have, had there been only one system of national education? You cannot dispute that for a moment. A short distance from where I live, in a good settlement, there are two schools, one a Roman Catholic separate school and the other, three-quarters of a mile away, a public school. The taxes of the people of that community are going to maintain two schools. It must be manifest to every person that the combined taxes of those people would maintain a far better school if there was only one; that both Roman Catholic and Protestant children would enjoy better educational advantages if there was only one school than they do at present with two schools. There is not only waste of money at present, but what is of more importance still, there is less efficiency in our school systems, because of this division. What choice has the family of a man got who happens to be living in a section of the country where nine-tenths of the people, we will say, happen to be Roman Catholics, and where the only school in the community is a separate school? What choice in the matter of education have the 'two or three Protestant families got who chance to be located there? The children are excluded from
that school unless the parents are willing to allow them to go there and hear religious dogma taught with which they do not agree.
I am not discussing whether that dogma is right or is wrong, but I-do say that the opinions of the minority should be respected and that the Protestant children are excluded from that school. What choice is open to the parents in such case? They must either send their children miles away from home and pay their board, or sell their farms and move to some other part of the country. How in the name of Heaven can you expect to obtain unity in this country when the children from two families-one a Roman Catholic family and the other a Protestant family, are going to different schools-one to this school and the other to that? Why, from the time they emerge from the cradle these children of opposite religious faith are taught to look with hostility and antagonism upon each other. How can you expect when they grow up to manhood that they can work together for the general welfare of this country? It is absolutely impossible; hon. gentlemen in this House, whether they favour separate schools or not, know that it is unfair and unreasonable to expect that they should.
I would favour first of all, Mr. Speaker, the creation of a Dominion bureau of education, because I believe the Dominion Government should have some voice in regard to educational matters. I would favour the holding of a conference in the city of Ottawa of leading educationists from the various provinces of Canada. Surely such men can come together on something which would promote the desired object, and surely they should come together. Surely we are within our rights as members of Parliament in advocating a condition of affairs where there will be some semblance of uniformity in teaching, because that uniformity in our public school teaching is necessary if we are to produce a united people in Canada animated by common national ideals.
This question, Sir, is one which affects, and very seriously, the people in Western Canada. According to the census of 1911 there were in the four Western Provinces 412,995 persons representing five nationalities,-Germans, Austrians, Russians, Poles and Scandinavians. Nearly half a million people of those five nationalities in those Western Provinces in 1911, and there are more than that number there now. We know to what extent we can rely upon those people in a crisis such as the one through which we have just passed. Should we not in the interests of the future welfare

of this country, try and devise some system whereby we will have some hope of Canadianizing these foreigners who come to our shores? But, Mr. Speaker; it is not only in regard to the West that I am speaking. May I call your attention to something very much nearer, something, it seems to me, that we ought to have at least a right to protest about? In 1912 a certain book was authorized for use in the schools in a part of this country. That book referred to Quebec as the capital of Canada, Toronto still figured as York, and Ottawa was not mentioned at all. Winnipeg did not even figure as Fort Garry; it was not even mentioned. The four Western Provinces are referred to in that book as "regions unknown except under the designation of New Caledonia, a wild region of no importance except for its furs." That is only an extract from the book in question. I could give the House other illuminating extracts if it was desired, but fancy a book being used in any province of Canady which issues such stuff as that to the children of this country at as recent a period as 1912. I do not know whether that book is still in use at the present time or not. Mr. Speaker, I believe it can be shown that text books have been used in the schools of this country lauding and praising Germany and Germans to the skies during the last four and a half years, while our boys have been overseas in France and Flanders giving up their lives in the struggle against those very people. Will any person tell me that the Federal Parliament has no right to intervene in a matter of that kind, and at least offer advice? I am perfectly well aware that there are some people in this country- like the hon. gentleman from Cape Breton (Mr. Butts) who interrupted me a while ago-who will not attempt to present any arguments on a question of this kind, who will not attempt to argue the subject on its merits, who *will not advance any reasons at all in support of their views, but will simply shout " bigotry " because they know it is the only expression which is applicable to themselves beyond the slightest doubt.
I do not care, Mr. Speaker, a snap of my fingers for the opinions of such people either in this House or outside of it. I have b':en honest in giving my views on this matter, because, Sir, I am a Canadian, and as a Canadian I would like to see a better state of affairs existing in this Dominion than has existed for many years. I would like to see more unity, more harmony, more peace-I would like to see our people of different races and creeds working shoulder to shoul-
der for the future well-being and upbuilding of this Dominion. It is because I do sincerely wish to see that desirable condition that I have given expression to these view's this afternoon, and I trust that hon. gentlemen either on this side or opposite will not find in anything I have said any attack on their religion. I have never in my life attacked the Roman Catholic faith.
Oh, oil.

Hon. gentlemen are free, of course, to offer the insult of a laugh. Yes, Mr. Speaker, I have been in this House for the last ten or eleven years, and I defy any hon. member to point to one single w'ord, line or sentence of mine uttered in this House reflecting on any man's religion. Now, laugh if you have got a laugh in you.
Oh, oh.

If hon. gentlemen opposite instead of laughing possess the quality of courage, let them get busy and present to me any statement of mine in this House or outside reflecting on any man's religion. I have never, Mr. Speaker, had any desire to reflect on any man's faith-never in my life, and I have never done so. But I will say to members of this House that when the Roman Catholic Hierarchy, or the Anglican Church, or the Presbyterian Church, or any other religious denomination through its ecclesiastical dignitaries sticks its nose into public affairs, I, as a public man, am going to hit that nose as I think it ought to be hit. Will any hon. gentleman tell me that on educational matters, on w'hich the Roman Catholic Hierarchy have very distinct views and have given expression to them-and they have a perfect right to do so-will hon. gentlemen tell me that as a public man I have no right to express my views? That is what I would assume from the attitude of at least one hon. gentleman judging by his expression a while ago. I have endeavoured to present this matter- which I repeat again I regard as of very great importance to the Dominion-in a series of statements very deliberately thought out, and again I invite hon. gentlemen to direct their attention and their arguments to some of those statements, which have been delivered with the best of intentions and without any ill-feeling towards any person, class or creed in this country.
Mr. JAMES A. ROBB (Chateauguay-Huntingdon): Mr. Speaker, wrn upon this side of the House did not have notice from my hon. friend that he was going to bring

up the resolution to-day. Indeed, it had been so long on the Order Paper that we had concluded that it might, like the Highways Bill, have fallen by the wayside. With his plea for national unity we upon this side are in common accord. There may be places in some of the provinces where there is not national unity, but I wish at once to assure my hon. friend that in the province of Quebec in which I live we have national unity.
My hon. friend (Mr. Edwards) seemed to be concerned more particularly regarding the school system in the province of Quebec, and for that reason I purpose to devote a few moments to an expression of my experience as a school trustee covering a period of perhaps twenty or
5 p.m. twenty-five years-longer than I care to remember. A few moments ago when my hon. friend was charging that there were schools in the province of Quebec which Protestants could not attend because of the religious training imparted, it brought to my mind a matter that I would rather not speak much about under these conditions, but in justice to my fellow citizens I am going to mention it. My only child for a number of years attended a Roman Catholic convent. As she was without a mother, naturally I watched very closely to see if any influence was brought to bear upon her, and I never was able to observe the slightest attempt to sway her religious feelings.

Might I ask the
hon. member a question? Did not the hon. member for Frontenac make it clear that he was speaking of primary schools?
No.

I am dealing with the question generally.. I have no knowledge that primary schools are any different in that respect from other schools. I have in mind places in the province of Quebec where there is perhaps only one school, a Protestant school, or a Catholic school as the case may be, and both Catholic and Protestant children are attending it. I was told not long ago by a prominent public man that all the education he had ever received was in a Roman Catholic school in the province of Quebec. That man is a Protestant and to-day occupies a very high position among the judiciary of the province of Ontario.
I do not want to get away from the main point. As I said, I have had an experience of from twenty to twenty-five years as a school trustee in the province of Quebec. We have at the opening of our
schools in the fall two difficulties: one difficulty is to provide sufficient space for the Roman Catholic French children who want to attend; the other difficulty is to get the newly-arrived Englishman to send his child to school instead of putting him in the local mill. In the town in which I live the local Roman Catholic college has three hundred boys in attendance, and there are many Protestant boys among them,-they go there because they wish to acquire the two languages,-and I have never heard that any attempt ever was made to influence their religious opinions.
But my hon. friend (Mr. Edwards) destroys his whole argument. He states that Article 93 of the British North America Act guaranteed separate schools to the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. Surely after all these years we are not going to reopen this question? If the hon. gentleman is sincere in his desire for peace and harmony throughout this country, I ask him in all fairness: can we accomplish that by reopening the question of religious training in schools? My hon. friend said that there might have been a better condition of things in this province of Ontario if the public	men of
the past had not been so cowardly In making that statement my hon. friend made a very serious attack upon that great statesman of whom he is a follower and admirer, and of whom we all are admirers, the late Sir John A. Macdonald. Sir John A. Macdonald had no such views as those entertained by the member for Frontenac. Listen to these words of that great statesman with regard to this school question, spoken in the House of Commons of Canada:
I have no accord with the desire expressed in some quarters that by any mode whatever there should be an attempt made to oppress the one language or to render it inferior to the other; I believe that would be impossible if it were tried and it would be foolish and wicked if it were possible. The statement that has been made so often that this is a conquered country is " a propos de rien." Whether it was conquered or ceded, we have a constitution under which all British subjects are in a position of absolute equality, having rights of ever} kind, of language, of religion, of property and of person. There is no paramount race in this country, there is no conquered race in this country, we are all British subjects, and those who are not English are none the less British subjects on that account.
That was the statement of a man who desired unity in this country, and it has the ring of true statesmanship. I submit in all seriousness that no good can be served by bringing this question up from time to time. My hon. friend seems to

think that Protestants in the province of Quebec are suffering. Let me, as a representative Protestant, assure him that we are perfectly satisfied with the system we now enjoy, and that we see great dangers ahead for us if the idea which the hon. gentleman presents to-day should prevail. Let me ask him, should we have national schools? Should we have one school as he suggests? What would be the language in the province of Quebec were his idea adopted? Where would the Protestants in that province stand? We are satisfied now with our school system; how would my hon. friend improve it?

I do not see any rea=on why the question of language should be brought in or how it affects the matter at all. If you had non-sectarian schools in Quebec, you would get along just as well so far as language is concerned. My idea is that the primary schools should be non-sectarian.

Very well; then the majority will rule. Only two or three years ago my hon. friend argued in this House that the schools in the province of Quebec were inferior, particularly that the Roman Catholic schools were inferior; and. that the Protestant schools in that province were much superior to the Roman Catholic schools. Does he want to put us back to the position he said we were in when he made that argument three years ago? If so, as a Protestant from Quebec, I cannot agree with him. Let me refer my hon. friend, who seems to be somewhat ignorant of the school laws of the province of Quebec, to the Acts upon which our school laws are founded. There is a Council of Public Instruction, composed of Roman Catholic and Protestant members. In the performance of their duties the members are subject to the lawful orders and instructions given to them by the Lieutenant Governor in Council. The Council of Public Instruction is divided into two committees, one composed of Roman Catholic members and the other of Protestant members. The Protestant Committee may associate with themselves six persons. and the Provincial Association of Protestant Teachers may each year at their annual meeting elect one of their members to be also an associate member of the Protestant Committee for the following year. The persons so added shall not form part of the Council of Public Instruction, but shall have in the Protestant Committee the same powers as the members of such Committee. School questions in which the interest of Roman Catholics and Protestants

are collectively concerned are under the jurisdiction of the Council of Public Instruction and shall be decided by it. That is fair; we are satisfied with that.
My hon. friend may think I am advancing a prejudiced idea; that I am making an argument simply because I am on the opposite side of the House. Let me put in evidence here" a statement of the Inspector General of Protestant schools in the province of Quebec. In 1914, in a pamphlet written by Dr. G. W. Parmelee the English or Protestant Secretary of the Council of Public Instruction, and Mr. J. C. Sutherland, Inspector General of Protestant Schools of the province, my hon. friend will find, at page 41, the following:
A perusal of the previous pages has probably made it clear that the Roman Catholic majority and the Protestant minority work harmoniously by dividing the educational regulations and administration into two separate parts in regard to all matters that would give rise to a conflict of opinion between them.
Inasmuch as these regulations include courses of study and provisions for religious instruction, and inasmuch as each committee approves of the textbooks for use in the schools of its own faith, ample guarantee is thus given to the Protestant minority that in vital matters the control of Protestant education will remain in Protestant hands, and at the same time the Roman Catholic Church is assured that religion in accordance with the tenets of the church shall continue to be inculcated as the basis upon which true education rests.
An annual meeting of the Dominion Educational Association was held in Ottawa in February, 1917. Mr. J. C. Sutherland, Inspector General of Protestant schools in the province of Quebec, attended that convention, and met there representatives from various parts of Ontario. At that convention he said:
There has never been a particle of friction in tffe department in this respect since Confederation or before that date	We (the
Protestant minority) have wonderful freedom, and whatever is needed is given. We never
have any trouble	We have a complete
system of reporting for the census, and also for the school attendance	
That is the evidence of a public servant who travels throughout the province of Quebec, covering a territory extending from a point 180 miles north of North Bay away down to the Gulf-Quebec is a big country. I am bound to say, therefore, that he has greater opportunity of learning the true feeling throughout the province of Quebec than has the member for Frontenac, who devotes most of his time to this House. As a Protestant from the province of Quebec, therefore, I certainly am not in favour of the resolution proposed by my hon. friend. Like him, I desire national unity. If

national unity does not prevail-in the other provinces of Canada, we wish to do all we can to bring it about. But in our province we get along very well, and we look with disfavour on any attempt to introduce anything that will change the good feeling now existing between the English-speaking and the French-speaking people, the Roman Catholics and the Protestants of my province.
Let me remind my hon. friend that as the basis of representation for all the provinces, Quebec is entitled to sixty-five members in this Parliament. Has it occurred to'him that almost twenty-four per cent of the representation in Parliament is Englishspeaking? That proves, it seems to me, that we get along fairly well from the school right up to manhood when we get into larger walks of life. So that I ask my hon. friend not to press a resolution which, in my judgment, can do no good and may do much harm.

I do not wish to add anything to what has been so well said on this subject by the member for Chateauguay-Hunting-lon (Mr. Robb) except to thank him, on behalf of his French Canadian colleagues in the House of Commons, for the fair statement that he has made. As for the member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) I am sorry that he thought it proper, having had his motion on the Order Paper since the beginning of the session, not to give notice to some of us that he would bring it up this afternoon.	, ~
But after all, it is just as well that the question came up as it did, because, while I do not wish to be unjust to my hon. friend, nor would I like to be severe on him, I do not think he has added much to his reputation by bringing, at this particular juncture, this irritating question before the public. It is more academic than anything else, if, indeed, it is anything else. The question of separate schools or nonsectarian schools was settled long ago, and I do not know, unless one has some special motive to serve, why one should start another school agitation at this very trying time in the history of our country.
The facts are, it seems to me, very simple. My hon. friend expresses the wish that we should have in Canada a non-sectarian school system, but the fact stares him in the face that the constitution of Canada, which he should respect as I respect it, settled that question in 1867, and if it may be said without offending my hon. friend, his study of Canadian history should lead
him to know that long before Confederation the question had been settled between fair-minded Canadians of both Taces and creeds. My hon. friend, a moment ago, said that Lord Durham had come to Canada with a very high mission and that he favoured the idea of having one set of laws, one language and one system of schools for Canada.

I did not mention
schools in connection with Lord Durham.

But my hon. friend, speaking of what was in Lord Durham's mind and what runs through his famous report, said that Lord Durham's idea was that we should have national unity in Canada, and Lord Durham, in his report, speaks of one language and of one law for Canada. My hon. friend added, if I followed him well, that if at that time we had had, pursuant to Lord Durham's mission, one system of schools, we would have had national unity in Canada. Indeed, Lord Durham had a very important mission when he came to Canada and he succeeded but only partly in his mission. One who reads his report must admit that in his now famous report he laid for us Canadians and members of the British Empire, the foundation of responsible government. In -that he succeeded, but when Lord Durham, radical though he was, expressed the opinion that there should be one code of laws and one language for the country, he made a fatal mistake, and that mistake is still very apparent to-day. Under the conditions which made this country British it cannot be expected that we shall ever have in 'Canada one system of laws for all the provinces, because the question was settled by the Act of Quebec in 1774, which Act we of the minority regard as our Magna Gharta. We must expect that as long as there is a French Canadian province in the Dominion there will be a different system of civil laws for French Canadians within their own province. That is an Imperial Statute, and we shall adhere to it. There is no danger that French Canadians will fall short in population; they are increasing yearly, and in so doing they are observing the command of God and of their conscience. As regards their language, let me say this without any boasting: As long as there beats a French heart we shall maintain intact the language which was given to us as a sacred legacy by our forefathers. It is a language of which any civilized man must be proud, because the French language, the language of Joffre, of Foch, of world diplomacy, is too noble a

language to be abandoned by those of us who represent French traditions and ideals in North America. My hon. friend said that if Lord Durham had insisted upon a system of non-sectarian schools-my hon. friend shakes his head-I take my hon. friend's denial in good part, and I say that the inference that I drew from his speech was that if Lord Durham had insisted at that time upon a system of non-sectarian schools we would have had true national unity in Canada. Sir, in 1841 French Canadians were in the majority in Lower Canada, but there was also in Lower Canada, the old French province, a respectable minority of English-speaking Protestants, as there was also in Upper Canada quite a minority of Catholics, both Irish and French. The common sense of the people of those early days settled the question without any statutory enactments. In Upper Canada there was a system of public schools, but the fair sense of the people agreed that there should be a separate school for those who wanted Catholic tuition for their children under Catholic supervision. In Lower Canada, notably in the Eastern Townships, there was, as I said, a Protestant minority, and there again the common sense and fairness of the people, without any special statutory enactment, decided that those Protestants should have their own schools. In 1841 the Union took place. It was not a success. The only thing which Union secured to Canada was responsible government, which had been fought for during and before the rebellion; and after 1841, thanks to the alliance of liberal-minded people from both Upper and Lower Canada, responsible government had to be conceded by, first, the Governor General, and finally by the Imperial authorities. But all those who are familiar with that period of our history know the wranglings that took place -Ee-tween both provinces and both parties during the period which elapsed between 1841 and 1867. Hon. Louis Joseph Papineau was then just back from exile. He had been brought back from Europe by Sir Hippolyte Lafontaine, and it is to his credit that in order to repatriate Hon. Louis Joseph Papineau he went even so far as to lay his resignation in the hands Of the then Governor General of Canada. Mr. Papineau came back again and began at once to agitate in favour of representation by population, because in his opinion the French representation should have been the largest, as the population of Lower Canada was the more numerous of the two.

Mr. Lafontaine, who afterwards became Sir Louis Hippolyte Lafontaine, took issue with Mr. Papineau, on the ground that the flow of British immigration would soon give Upper Canada the majority, and when that happened we could not expect a larger representation for Lower Canada. Later on, events proved that Mr. Lafontaine's attitude was the right one, but in the meantime the school question became very acute. The School Act of 1855 was first passed, and then the Act of 1863, an Act which had been fathered by Mr. Scott, who later became Secretary of State under the Laurier Government, which position he also occupied 18 years before under the Mackenzie Government. The legislation of 1863 enacted practically what was later embodied in the Act of Confederation itself. Mr. Brown was then a member of the legislature, and he tenaciously opposed the separate school system. Long and acrimonious discussions took place, and as my hon. friend said a moment ago the leader of the Conservative party, Sir John Macdonald, himself favoured a system of separate schools for Upper and Lower Canada in order that the Protestant minority in the province of Quebec and the Catholic minority in the province of Ontario might be protected. Later on, when Government under the Union became a failure, because every ministry changed after three or four months in office, Mr. Brown again took up the question of representation by population and advocated Confederation as the only solution compatible with the principles which had been advocated by Mr. Papineau. The English minority had then become the majority. Mr. Brown was so insistent on the question of Confederation that I think I am within the mark when I say that he was really the man who did most to achieve the anactment of 1867, but in order to succeed, Mr. Brown, nobly I must say, accepted a compromise on the vexed school question. In 1863, and in fact all throughout the regime of the Union from 1841 to 1863, Mr. Brown had been the most vigorous opponent of the separate school system and had carried with him the bulk of his party in Upper Canada. But Mr. Brown knew that in order to achieve Confederation he had to make some sacrifice of opinion, some concession, that he must accept a compromise. And what was the nature of that compromise? I would point out to the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards! that at times, especially in a country like this with its two great races, where there are different creeds and languages it is fair, it is well that.there should be com-

promise. Mr. Brown, who was a statesman, understood that. I dare say there has never been a man in Canada who was more insistent on non-sectarian schools than the late Hon. George Brown. Indeed, his paper, the Toronto Globe, and before that the Leader, every day contained articles written by Mr. Brown advocating his view of non-sectarian schools. But in 1867, in order to achieve the higher idea! of Confederation Mr. Brown accepted a compromise. I have here his very words which I shall read, in part, to the House. Speaking on clause 6, which read as follows :
Education, saving the rights and privileges which the Protestant or Catholic minority in both Canadas may possess as to their denominational schools at the time when the union goes into operation.
Mr. Brown said:
I need hardly remind the House that I have always opposed and continue to oppose the system of sectarian education, so far as the public chest is concerned. I have never had any hesitation on that point, I have never been able to see why all the people in the province, to whatever sect they may belong, should not send their children to the same schools to receive the ordinary branches of instruction. I regard the parent and the pastor as the best religious instructors-and so long as the religious faith of the children is not interfered with, and ample opportunity afforded to the clergy to give religious instruction to the children of their flocks, I cannot see any sound objection to mixed schools.
Further on he says:
Now, it is known to every hon. member of this House that an Act was passed in 1863 as a final settlement of this sectarian controversy. I was not in Quebec at the time, but if I had been here, I would have voted against that Bill because it extended the facilities for establishing separate schools. Does my hon. friend

Practically the same.
I am citing the opinion of Mr. Brown in order to show how he compromised on the separate school question, in order to achieve the higher ideal of Confederation. He went on:
When, therefore, it was proposed that a provision should be inserted in the confederation scheme to bind that contract of 1863 and declare it a final settlement, so that we should not be compelled, as we have been since 1849,
to stand constantly to our arms, awaiting fresh attacks upon our common school system, the proposition seemed to me one that was not rashly to be rejected. I admit that, from my point of view, this is a blot on the scheme before the House ; it is confessedly, one of the concessions from our side that had to be made to secure this great measure of reform. The opinion of Sir John A. Macdonald has already been quoted by my hon. friend, and I have now given 'the opinion of his great antagonist and rival, the Hon. George Brown. The one had already committed himself in favour of separate schools for the sake of national unity, and the other accepted them by force majeure, I must say, but in order to achieve Confederation. But my hon. friend went further, and though I will follow him in his arguments, in doing so I do not intend to re-open the debate on the famous Autonomy Bill. In Manitoba the system of 'separate schools was established when that province entered Confederation. We all remember the agitation which followed., We know that those who represented the minority in Parliament and outside sought to obtain justice for the Catholics of Manitoba. Finally a settlement was arrived at known as the Laurier-Greenway settlement. It was, indeed, a settlement based on the minimum of rights and yet the minority accepted it, some with loud protests .and others in the hope and expectation that the majority would at least live up to the agreement. I regret to say that twenty-three years after, a so-called Liberal Government in Manitoba has thought it wise to wipe out the Laurier-Greenway agreement and to treat the French Canadian minority in that province on a foating of equality with the foreign immigrants who have no such constitutional guarantee as has the minority which joined Confederation with Manitoba.
Did not the Laurier-Greenway settlement put the foreigner on the same footing as the French?

Yes, hut was it just, was it fair that the Norris Government as they did three years ago should enact legislation wiping out all such moderate terms as' were agreed upon in the Laurier-Greenway agreement? I leave it at that. History will pronounce judgment on the action of the majority. History will say if it was the true British spirit which instigated Mr. Norris, and before him Mr. Roblin and the others, in curtailing every year, until they wiped them out entirely, the minimum rights which had been secured under the Laurier-Greenway agreement. Mr. Speaker, the resolution introduced this afternoon by the member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) is a very important one. In rising to address the House as its seconder, I realize that many people in this country will consider it as not belonging to the arena of federal politics. They will say that the question of education is entirely provincial, and that the Fedejal Government has nothing whatever to do with it. But the Act passed by the Fathers of Confederation in 1867 can hardly be said to stand for all time with regard to education, when condi-vtions in the country are changing. The Fathers of Confederation scarcely had a glimpse of the great progress which had been made since that time in all affairs, especially in the scientific world. We are living to-day under different conditions; we are not the same people that we were in 1867; consequently, this question of national non-sectarian schools is very appropriate at the present time.
Public opinion must first be educated to accept measures which are vital to a country's growth before popular support will warrant their incorporation in the statutes. There must be a demand, a compelling force behind a movement in order to make it a success. That there is such a demand-a growing demand-all over this country for non-sectarian national schools, no one will deny. That demand has been growing for a number of years; it has become intensified during the period of the war. Great events change the current of the people's thoughts and suddenly illuminate the public mind to popular defects that act as barriers to national progress. The day has gone by when the British North America Act is regarded as unchangeable, like the laws of the Medes and Persians; if it contains clauses which are inimical to our progress and our unity, those clauses should be removed.
The British North America Act passed in 1867 by the Imperial Parliament, is the constitution of the Dominion of Canada. That constitution was brought about by a compromise between the two races living in this country at that time, and who came together on an agreement under which Confederation
was made possible. I do not intend, Mr. Speaker, to advocate that that agreement should be dealt with as only a scrap of paper. I believe that it is possible that all the provinces of this Dominion can come together on -a system of national, nonsectarian schools which will be satisfactory to all. Such a consummation of this question is eminently to be desired.
A great national spirit has been born out of the travail of this war and Canada has burst into nationhood. Our sphere has suddenly become larger and we stand before the world to-day as one of the great nations of the future, where yesterday we were unknown. We are no longer a loosely connected system of provinces, largely interested in provincial affairs, jealous of one another, fearful of our special prerogatives, looking to the Federal Government for preferment and acknowledging it as our only tie of union. A great unifying national spirit pervades all the people of the various provinces. A trail of blood crosses this country from ocean to ocean, uniting the many diverse elements in our population with a tie that the lapse of time can only serve to strengthen. The war brought us one of the greatest opportunities in our history, if we but utilize it to the full. What this country needs in the present critical hour is a man, a statesman with a vision, who can give the people a common objective and a lofty ideal of national life. Every nation has a destiny, a destiny which is founded upon the character of its people, guided by the will of God. Every nation that is worthy of the name has a soul. It cannot, properly speaking, be called a nation until it manifests that soul. Canada has a soul; the war revealed it. It is the collective soul of her people, and as the people are, so is the nation. The individual characteristics of a people find expression in their national life and determine the nation's status in world affairs. If Canada is to take a high place among democratic peoples, we must have leadership of a high order to concentrate public sentiment and public service on well-defined lines of national endeavour.
The average man and the average woman should be enabled to visualize our future. This implies education of all the people on broad, national lines; education in everything that goes to make the name "Canadian" mean character. Canada has the nucleus of a national character now. . When our soldiers and nurses appeared on the European battlefields, they were quickly recognized as

representing a distinctly Canadian type. This was not noticeable twenty-five years ago; when we were submerged in the general term "American." Owning the same cosmopolitan parentage as our cousins to the south, we are not like them. That difference is growing more marked year by year. Neither are we like the Europeans, from whom we have sprang. Climate, environment, the blending of nationalities and the natural obstacles with which we cope, have left their impress upon our character and mark us out as a people having a distinct destiny of our own. In the working out of that destiny the elementary schools of our country will take a high place. Our public school is the most vital factor in the formation of Canadian character. It is the crucible into which the polyglot population of this country is thrown, mixed together, ground up and moulded into the finished product of Canadian citizenship. Peoples of all languages, races and creeds go into that crucible and must be subjected to the moulding process in order that Canada may work out her destiny among the nations.
Our public school, then, is a national issue, and should be made a national institution, purely Canadian, and undenominational in its character. Anything that interferes with its efficiency in turning out Canadians imbued with a love for home and country is detrimental to the future of Canada. Any influence that favours segregation, that divides our population into classes on any claim of expediency, of selfinterest, of community interest, or of denominational interest, is dangerous and obnoxious and is bound to re-act to our national dishonour and our national disintegration.
This country has a great future. We have all the elements of a great nation-a vast extent of territory, illimitable resources of a diversified character; millions of acres of arable land stretching from ocean to ocean; a large system of inland waterways of great commercial importance; vast stretches of forest country; great areas of lands containing minerals of all kinds; a climate which is conducive to a hardy, virile race, and a dominating Canadian personality that has placed its hall-mark on our native-born population. This country is in the eye of the world as never before, and an ever increasing stream of immigrants from war-swept Europe will continue to find its way to our shores. These people will come here with pre-con-ceived opinions of freedom of government, and with revolutionary ideals.
[Mr. Anderson.!
They will come here with social and religious opinions as varied as the people themselves. They will come here representing all grades of humanity, the fit, the unfit, and the misfits, asking for an opportunity to live out their allotted span on the virgin soil of Canada. If we admit them-and I submit, Mr. Speaker, we must admit them, by a selective process, if you will-then we must shoulder the responsibility for their education, future protection and support.
The North American continent has been the melting pot for the surplus population of Europe for two centuries. As has been so well said, the nineteenth century belonged to the United States, and the twentieth century will belong to the Dominion of Canada. The words of the Acting Prime Minister (Sir Thomas White), that within fifteen years we may have a population of 20,000,000 people, are prophetic. I believe it is within easy distance of this country to attain by a progressive immigration policy. These surplus peoples have been and will be flung promiscuously into the arms of Canada that she may take them to her broad bosom and make them her own. They do not come here by accident, not by any mere chance, but in the fulfilment of a Divine plan. The hand of destiny directs their course, and the finger of destiny points the way for Canada to link her future with theirs.
How best to assimilate them, to transform them into good, law-abiding progressive citizens, is the problem this country must solve; and we expect Union Government to adopt a national policy on this question, to throw down the barriers of race and religion and to unite our people in a common national ideal that will consolidate this country from coast to coast into a permanent Canadian entity. The Dominion Government cannot shirk the issue by delegating it to the provinces, but should co-operate with the provinces in co-ordinating our school system on a national basis, having for its object the assimilation, of the foreigner, the blending of nationalities, and the formation of a permanent Canadian type that will stamp its mentality forever on the Land of the Maple.
Education, then, is the imperative duty of the State. We may as well face the situation that confronts us to-day and prepare for eventualities. Everything points to further disturbances the world over. There is no permanent peace in sight. The world is in a dangerous mood; Europe is seething with revolution, and our foreign element is restless in sympathy with their home coun-

tries. Nothing prevents Bolshevism from raising its ugly head in this country but the scattered condition of its votaries, and the sane attitude of our industrial class, combined with the efforts of the Government to give employment to the masses. I compliment the Government on its progressive policy in this respect. It is worthy of the support of every man who has the welfare of his country at heart. Bolshevism is autocracy in reaction. We have had many examples of it in the world, but the latest one is Russia. A people held under the leash of autocratic restraint for centuries suddenly find their bonds are severed and rush to the opposite extreme of lawlessness, rapine and murder. Every man his own lawmaker; human passions unrestrained, surge and flow in the widest confusion, reducing the immortal soul of man to a depth of degradation beneath the lowest grade of the brute creation. -Russia to-day exhibits to a shuddering world the most beastly spectacle of human depravity that ever stained the pages of history. Nothing remains but to confine them within their own boundaries until their passions recoil in horror from their terrible excesses. Bolshevism is rooted in ignorance. Ignorance is slavery, a slavery that fetters the intellect and stunts the soul. Let this country rise to the occasion and baffle (his mediaeval monster masquerading under the guise of freedom. Education on broad lines of justice and truth is the remedy, Education of all our people without regard to the restraints of race or religion is the only hope of democracy. We often hear the statement made that democracy must be made safe for the people, but, Mr. Speaker, democracy is the people, and the people must be educated in order to be safe for democracy. The greatest guarantee for the security of life and property is education. If you inculcate into the youthful mind a love for the eternal principles of truth and justice, democracy will take care of itself.
