I ask because it is generally understood that Sweden has no illiterates at all. I do not know whether that is true, and I only ask for information.

Perhaps that is why Sweden is not in the list I saw. Australia's percentage is 1.8; New South Wales, 2 per cent; New Zealand, .9 per cent; Queensland, 2.5 per cent. I believe that these figures will indicate that the countries that have national non-sectarian schools have the least illiteracy. The percentage of illiterates in Australia, which has non-sectarian schools, is 1.8, while North America-the United States and Canada-we have as high as 7.7 and 11.45.
The census of 1911 shows that there was a total population in the Dominion of 7,206,643, of whom 54.08 per cent were British, 28.5 French, and 17.41 foreign horn. There were 752,732 foreign-born in Canada in 1911, and of these 62 per cent were in the four western provinces. Of these foreigners, 45.77 per cent were naturalized, and 54.23 per cent were aliens. The percentage of foreign-born in the leading cities is as follows: Toronto, 8.8; Montreal, 9.2; Hamilton, 9.4; Calgary, 20; Edmonton, 22; Regina, 22.6; Winnipeg, 24.2; Vancouver, 27.6, and Fort William, 28.2. This will demonstrate that the larger part of our foreign element is in the country west of the Great Lakes.
From the same census I find that the people belong to religious denominations as follows: Presbyterians, 1,115,324; Methodists, 1,079,892; Anglicans, 1,043,017; other Protestants, 457,470, making a total of 3,735,703. Roman Catholics, 2,833,041; Greeks, 88,507, a total of 2,921,548. This does not take into consideration the other denominations which can scarcely be classed as Protestants or- Roman Catholics, and

which make up a small part of our population. These various people were divided among 72 religious denominations.
From these figures it will be seen that ihe hula of our foreign-born immigrants are in ihe Western Provinces. Of the naturalized foreigners, 71.85 per cent are in the Western Provinces; that is, more are naturalized in the Western Provinces than in the East; 16.01 per cent in Ontario and 2.19 per cent in the Maritime Provinces. It will also be seen that Canada is overwhelmingly British in its population, and it is likely to remain so on account of the sane immigration legislation introduced by the present Government. I believe it is in the interests of this country that that should be so. The Anglo-Saxon race has placed its mark indelibly on the North American continent. The language, the customs, and the habits are theirs. English is spoken by 110.000,000 people on the North American continent, and by four-fifths of the people in the Dominion of Canada. It is essential to the economic and social welfare of every citizen of this country that he should be able to speak that language; otherwise, he will be under a very serious handicap. This does not mean the exclusion of other languages from our public or private life. I believe that the French language which has a hold in this country should be taught; it is a beautiful language, and I am only sorry that I cannot speak it myself. I do not think any person in this country should be debarred from speaking or studying that language, and there should be no objection to it being taught in our national schools.
A national non-sectarian school is not a question of religion or of race, but a question of what kind of education in the interests of the country as a whole shall the State provide for the children in our public schools, for the maintenance of which all the people are taxed without regard to race or creed. Experience tells us that this education should be of a harmonizing, unifying character, blending the children of our cosmopolitan population together with common aims and common hopes. That being the case, has the State any duty to perform in regard to education in our public schools. That question will be answered in the affirmative by four-fifths of the people in this country.
As we have at least 72 different religious denominations in Canada, it is not in the interests of this country that any one of those denominations should be singled oat for special privilege. Such special privi-

lege is a signal for distrust and attack. Tihe system is vicious in principle, and dangerous in practice. To give concessions to a minority because it' is a minority is entirely wrong. What is good for the majority should be equally good for the minority. It is claimed that the Protestant minority in the province of Quebec have been granted the same privileges as the Roman Catholic minority in the province of Ontario in thqir public schools; I think hon. gentlemen opposite have said so today, and I believe it is correct. I believe that the Protestants have the same privileges in the schools of the province of Quebec as the Roman Catholics have in the province of Ontario. This may appear fair on the surface, but it works out rather to the disadvantage of the Protestants. In Ontario the Roman Catholic children have the privilege of going to the public school if there is no separate school in their parish. There they receive a good common education on secular subjects without any interference whatever with their religion; there is no attempt whatever to give them any religious instruction. But in the province of Quebec, if the Protestant sends his children to the Roman Catholic school, they are always hearing the religion of that faith taught in the school. They are not compelled to study it, but they are young and their minds are impressionable, and when they hear this religion taught repeatedly they gain a certain insight into a faith which their parents are not in sympathy with. Consequently, it works out rather to the disadvantage of the Protestant.
The parochial, or separate, or confessional, schools-call them what you will- are getting some hold in the Canadian West, particularly among the foreign element which have these schools in their own country. These schools are a relic of the past, and it would be a retrograde movement to have them established in this country. The struggle for secular schools has been long and "bitter, and the fruits of that struggle should not be endangered. The parochial school is usually under the control of some particular denomination and is inclined to be narrow in its character. It places too much stress on the teaching of religious subjects without teaching religion, and its main object is to perpetuate ecclesiastical control.
Parochial schools favour segregation and prevent that social intercourse which is productive of friendly relationship. They are
productive of class interests and class hatred. They divide the people on racial apd religious lines and retard assimilation. The parochial school, as we have it in this country, is almost entirely racial and in that sense is unnational. It favours disruption rather than unity. Unless under strict supervision by the education authorities it is a menace to the future peace and progress of this country. This is more clearly seen in relation to the great tide of immigration which is coming to our shores. In the Canadian West there are foreign communities, people coming from foreign lands, from the autocratic countries of Europe, living in communities where they have their own churches, papers, schools, and stores, and speaking their own language to the exclusion of the French and English languages. Democracy can have no chance in a com

munity such as that. These people are the representatives of autocratic countries in Europe and they are propagating the ideas they imbibed there. There is no Cana-dianization going on amongst them, assimilation is at a standstill, and it is not by that means that they can be made into good Canadian citizens. You will find these communities in different parts of the West. Communities of Ruthenians can be found in Manitoba near Gimli, Sifton, Starbuck and Shore Lake; in Saskatchewan near Kenora, Rosthern and Vonda, and in Alberta near Starz and Pakan, northeast of Edmonton.
I am aware, Mr. Speaker, that it is a difficult matter to prevent these communities from forming. These people want to live together and our own Canadian element is not desirous of living amongst them. But I contend that these people should be compelled to have our public schools in their midst, that they should be taught the English language, and the responsibilities of Canadian citizenship and be made acquainted with our laws. If we ever want to make them citizens of this country we must exact these conditions. We are handing out to these people the vote when they have absolutely no knowledge of what a vote means. They are simply parts of autocratic Europe scattered over our Canadian-West and living in the heart of a democratic country.
The British North America Act, as I said before, was a compromise between the two dominating nationalities inhabiting this country at the time of Confederation. The object of this Act was unity; the intention of the Fathers of Confederation was to effect such a confederation of the provinces

as it was fondly hoped would unite the various parts of British North America on terms of equality and unity. It was hoped that the races would in time amalgamate into common entity and become what they must ultimately become, a distinctly Canadian type. Neither race should dominate the other; in fact, neither race will dominate the other but all races represented in this country must fuse imperceptibly into each other so that Canada may fulfil the great destiny intended for her in the civilization of the world. There is little use to kick against the pricks; an inexorable fate shapes our course. Time and the tide of immigration coming to our shores will ultimately break down all harriers and leaven the whole into one common mould.
That leavening process has gone on and is making considerable progress; so much so in fact that there is a Canadian type easily recognized now. But so far as the two dominating races are concerned, there is no fusion and there is only the semblage of unity. The British North America Act is a failure in this respect. After fifty years trial this must be admitted by any impartial judge. The alignment of this House proves it. The cause of the present cleavage is significant and demands an explanation. Unless the cause is found the remedy cannot be applied. I belifeve it to be in our educational system. Our schools are too narrow in their scope. They are too provincial. They fail to take that broad national character which can visualize Canada as a whole and which is productive of sound Canadian citizenship. The main object of our schools is to produce Canadians worthy of their greatest heritage, Canadians pure and simple, not Englishmen or Frenchmen, not Protestants or Roman Catholics, but Canadians without regard to race or creed. The public school then is a national issue. It is imperative that we have a national policy on education.
In the working out of our school system the personalty of and the equipment of the teacher should not be overlooked. The teacher is the greatest benefactor in the land -the school-mistress and the school-master are the pillars of civilization-without whom this old world would soon revert to barbarism ; and yet there Is no class of public servants so shamefully underpaid. There is very little to tempt them to begin and nothing to induce them to remain.
During this reconstruction period when old superstitions and social fallacies are being swept aside with such astonishing swiftness, something should be done to

raise this important profession to the high financial standard its usefulness deserves, so that our returned soldiers many of whom have already nearly qualified may be tempted to enter the profession. I would respectfully draw the attention of the Government to the importance of giving these men every assistance to induce them to enter the teaching profession. None are so capable to give our public schools and high schools that patriotic atmosphere which is so essential to the production of sound Canadian citizenship.
There will be many monuments erected by a grateful people to the memory of our heroic soldiers. These monuments will be placed in the most prominent positions in every city and town across this broad country. They will represent the local ideas and will be representative of the community characteristics of the people. They will take many forms in accordance with the diversity of opinion in the various sections interested. An effort should be made to make them as beautiful in form and as lasting in material as skill can erect.
Canada is a young country but already rich in inspiring traditions which should be kept well before the notice of our growing population. These monuments will have a great educational value. Their importance in this respect should not be overlooked. The creation of a patriotic national sentiment is inseparable from them. They point to our part played in the great struggle for human liberty which has just been brought to a successful conclusion. They twill inspire future generations to emulate the heroic self-sacrifice and loyalty to the Empire of our young men who so promptly came forward to offer their services in defence of human liberty.
A day should be set apart as a national holiday for the decoration of these monuments. A suitable day for this purpose would be the day on which peace is signed by the great powers. It will come at a time of the year when flowers are available and the weather suitable for outside celebration, a day on which it is fondly hoped the dove of peace on expectant wings will slowly settle down on a blood-stained world. Veterans of the Great War could have reunions, and the public could meet to hear patriotic addresses having for their purpose the intensifying of a national sentiment, in which this country is deficient.
The graves of our heroic dead 3,000 miles away cannot be decked with the flowers which loving hands would fain place on them. These monuments could be decorated

"In Memoriam" of them with flowers, and this would give the occasion that touch of solemnity necessary to deep, abiding sentiment. Canada is commencing a new era of untold possibilities. We can only glimpse our wonderful potentialities by taking a mental vision of the years ahead. A hundred millions of people will inhabit this country in less than a century, and they will be a people which only a northern clime can produce, a people who will sway the civilized world with their wealth and commercial power. The foundation is now being laid, and it is the supreme duty of the hour for all our people to unite in giving up racial and religious differences and in laying the foundation on the rocks of truth, justice and honour.

In the discussion of this subject I have already been criticised adversely by many friends who say that by national schools we aim a blow at civil and religious liberty; that we seek to increase the influence of the Dominion Government; that we are unconstitutional; and those who know my constituency best say that I am, by speaking on the subject, sealing my political damnation. I do not propose to argue any of the objections made to national schools unless those objections are supported by sound arguments. So far as the unconstitutionality of this question is concerned, the consent of the province will remove all difficulties in the way; and so far as my political damnation is concerned in my own constituency, if to occupy a public position means that a man is going to sacrifice his personal conviction and be a slave to factions moved by personal interest, bias, bigotry or religious narrowness, then somebody else can be the slave, for I prefer not to have the unenviable distinction.
We have heard in this House during the present session a number of men who have been wont to speak of the Society of Nations as though Canada was a nation, when, as a matter of fact it is not, in spite of what may be said by opportunist poli-ticans who seek to foist upon us as realities the dreams of their political and speculative imagination. Granting, however that Canada enjoys the status of a nation, I am going to ask you, Mr. Speaker, 'the following question:	Does it constitute a
nation to have a collection of warring provinces? I am willing to grant you, for the sake of argument, that we have the full status of nationhood. Are we then a nation when you find various provinces viewing important questions of public life
in Canada through different glasses? What then, you may ask, is a nation? It is defined as an agglomeration of men, of people, who have had the same love and the same hatred; who have tasted the same joys, and undergone the same reverses; who revere the same great historical figures; who salute the same flag, and interpret its meaning in the same way, because they have received in the same school the same mentality; in other words, an agglomeration of men whose intellectual, moral and political formation is the same. Sir Martin Conway defines a nation as follows:
What in fact is a nation? It is not merely a number of individuals dwelling within a particular geographical area, nor a population talking a common language, nor is it to be defined by the possession of a common stock or blood-relationship. A nation is the whole population of an area, organized into a single crowd by the possession of a common ideal. It is patriotism that makes a nation, not vice versa. Thus Africanders will be a nation, if they are not so already, when their feeling of unity overpowers and submerges their attachment to their component race-crowds. There is no reason even to desire an individual to forget whether he is of British or Dutch origin. That is an immaterial detail once the passion of the overcrowd is stronger than that of the section. When that has been brought about a nation exists; and the common ideal once created is liable to grow into that kind of passion which, as Mr. Tim Healy informed Mr. Winston Churchill, can be recognized when it shows itself to be ' something that men willingly die for.'
Now, Mr. Speaker, geographical location, language, race, religion, and economic conditions are not essential factors in the formation of a nation. The Jewish nation is as real as any, yet it is scattered all over the world. Switzerland speaks many languages, and no one will deny that Switzerland is a nation. Two religions hold equal sway in Germany without menacing the existence of the German nation. Two absolutely distinct races inhabit Belgium, and yet we salute with respect the Belgian nation. So far as the economic side is concerned, were not the Germans more attached to their own people than to the Poles, with whom they had the most lucrative commercial relations? The essential primordial factor in the formation of a nation is mentality; and no matter what may be the geographical location, religion, race or economic conditions of the Canadians, if they possess the same mentality, then, and then only, will they be a nation. The national school, according to my view, is the instrument with which to accomplish efficiently and successfully this object. How can the people of Ontario, Quebec, the western provinces, and the Maritime

Provinces discuss harmoniously the rights and the duties of the citizen, the family, and the state, df they possess three or four different mentalities; the flag of Canada means a different thing to each group. Let me give you a few examples of this most perplexing question. In 1884, at the time of the Sudan war the flag meant one thing to the French and another thing to the English. In 1889 at the time of the Boer war the same thing occurred. In 1914 the message of the flag was heard for the third time, and you know the results as well as I do. A certain author says:
Narrowness, provincialism, bigotry, describe a personality in which unity of purpose is won at the sacrifice of breadth, outlook and sympathy. The highest type of personality grows out of many far-reaching selves which have been selected and organized into unity by a dominant purpose. It is no easy task to unify often divergent and conflicting impulses, habits, memories and ideals into a harmonious heir-archy of aims. But such singleness of ideal and effort creates power. The ideal personality includes many selves organized by a masterful purpose and unified by a spirit of harmony.
Buskin says:
Education does not mean teaching people to know what they do not know-it means teaching them to behave as they do not behave.
The French are probably more fortunate in the use of language. They have two words for the English " Education In French the word education means the bringing up, the conduct of people in the sense referred to by Buskin, and they use the word " instruction " for the learning which a person may gain. " I will do it," promises a South African. " On the word of an Englishman?" inquires his friend. " Yes, on the word of an Englishman ". That is the finest tribute to the English public school and the English university that the country affords. That emphasizes absolutely what we should have in this nation when I speak of mentality, that people should so conduct themselves that their word is their bond, that it means everything.
Let me ask you candidly this question: Are you going to profit by the triple experience of 1884, 1899 and 1914 and lay the foundation of a school system, the result of which will be that my boy in the western provinces will have the same mentality as the boys of Ontario, Quebec and the Maritime Provinces; or, far from changing your views with regard to the primordial factor in the formation of a nation, will you continue to invade our western provinces with your retrograde mentalities because they are provincial and so create unfortunate reactions?

I do not agree entirely with previous speakers when they refer to a national non-sectarian school. Why is it that the eye of God to-day, the only sanction of true morality, has been replaced in some of our western schools by the eye of the world,-a Pharisaical sanction; unless it be on account of the machinations of opportunist politicians who seek to place on our children the yoke of their respective religious organizations? Is there in this country a single thinker who would not be willing to make provincial sacrifices in order to endow the whole Dominion with a school system based on knowledge, respect and love of God? All nations that have achieved greatness, which still lives although the nations themselves may have disappeared, and whose thought still en-ohants the world-the Greeks and the Bo-mans,-taught in their schools their children the knowledge, respect and love of God, who punishes the nations and individuals who transgress and rewards those who observe the principles of right and justice. If the non-sectarian school means that you are to ignore these fundamental principles, I could not support it.
Mr. Speaker, some people say that it is a question of the preservation of laws. I say it is not, for laws are merely the expression of facts, and, consequently, are transient. It is not a question of clinging to this or that organized church. We all know in what sect we were born and initiated, but after twenty, thirty or forty years can any man state with certainty to what creed he adheres? To quote the great Newman: "To live is to change; and to be perfect is to have changed often."
One of the previous speakers has given the key-note of what is expected of Canadians so far as the future is concerned, and in that connection I would like to read you what a returned soldier said regarding education. I quote from an article written by Capt. L. H. Lang in The Western Veteran of November 16 last:
That means to say that the real task that lies before Canada to-day is the building up of a free and vigorous national spirit which will bring to her a great position amongst the nations of the world. No greater task has ever faced1 a country before. The days, too, of sectarianism are over and gone. Those of us who have been out to the Front are appalled andl disgusted by the sight of churches whose duty it is to bear witness to a God of Love, dissipating their energy upon their little points of difference rather than presenting a united front against the powers of evil and self-oentredness. The churches exist not for their own advancement or material success, but they exist to show the world at large the

road to a higher, deeper and more beautiful conception of human fellowship.
That is true of men who have been abroad and witnessed for themselves the political organizations which reside within their own churches.
It is said that national schools imply a question of language. I wish not to be misinterpreted in this regard because I state that it is not a question of language. Nature has settled that question in the valley of the St. Lawrence for all time to come with all its political, social and economic consequences. But, of course, it would be imprudent, it would be unpardonably clumsy, yes, it would be 9 p.m. politically suicidal to allow certain affective, mystical and collective illusions to die out in Canada. I stated some time ago in this House that I knew a constituency in Alberta where there are three absolutely distinct national mentalities supplied by three different school systems, thanks to the methodical issue of permits. The member for that constituency has a triple political organization-English, Frendh and Russian. When the fight is on they go forth with three battle cries. When among the English at Boyne Lake and Ashmount it is " Long live the British Empire"; then at Plamond-ville and Lac Labiche it is " Long live Quebec"; and when at Cache Lake and other Ruthenian centres it is " Russia for ever." You can quite understand that^ the member himself does not stoop to these religious .and racial prejudices, but his organization is doing this work. There you see this system in all its crudity, and you appreciate how full of turpitude it is. If the school system in Alberta, for instance, permits this kind of thing, what can you expect of the rising generation? If to-day you have the Ukrainians of Western Canada petitioning the Dominion Government to establish national schools, it is because they were told they could have their separate schools just as the French have their primary course in the schools of the West. It is because the Government of each province has exploited the people for political reasons and has left them to-day under the impression that they are to be deported. When those people ask why they should be deported the answer is, that they have not become assimilated. They are not Canadians. The result is that having been cajoled into this unfortunate position by politicians, they are asking the Dominion Government to take hold of this question and to give them national education so they can become Canadianized.
The Western Provinces differ somewhat from the Eastern Provinces in the matter of education. We have a large number of Americans coming in there, and often those men get permits to teach school the same as men from other provinces receive permits to teach in different languages, sometimes carrying on a French school entirely, sometimes a Russian. If you wish to keep the provinces united, if you wish to keep Confederation intact, it is necessary that something should be done in the way of education for our Western Provinces. We are being Americanized at a rapid rate, as will be admitted by every member from the West. At the present time if you go through the streets of some of our Western cities you will find the boys wearing a button on the lapel of their coats with the words, " We did it." Do you think any Canadian would be allowed to wear such a button on his coat in New York or in any of the other large cities of the United States?
The American would see that the bottom was removed. But out in the Western Provinces we do not pay any attention to these things. We are being Americanized, and it is not necessary that we should have a national school or some sort of schools to replace those of the present day.
I do not know whether all the facts have been given in connection with the literacy of the Western Provinces and of Canada as a whole, but something of interest struck me the other day when I was reading one of the local newspapers. It was the statement that four million American-born children never learned to read and write. The article goes on to say:-
100.000	of our public school teachers are only 19 years old.
50.000	of them are without high school education.
The salary of a graduate teacher is no more than that of a milliner's apprentice while she is learning her trade.
An article by H. Addington Bruce deals with the American situation so far as teachers are concerned. I venture to say that what is true of the United States is true also of Canada, and more particularly of Western Canada. Young girls receive from $60 to $80 a month to teach in a school which is 150 or 200 miles from any large centre. Probably she is from sixteen to nineteen years of age, possessing only a permit, or sometimes the requisite diploma. How can children of this age-because they are children in reality-impart Canadian mentality to the younger men and women of the country? A girl of sixteen or eighteen

has to teach boys, Russians and Ruthenians, of twenty-two and twenty-three. These young people require more than the attention of a girl of sixteen to nineteen.
Again, how can you expect education in the Western Provinces to be properly carried out by teachers who do not intend to make teaching a profession? It is a fact that most young men and women who teach do not intend to make teaching a profession. With the man, it is a stepping-stone to the study of medicine or of some other profession; with the girl, it is only an interim occupation which she is prepared to give up at any time for a suitable marriage. In my opinion, the Government of Canada has as much to do with the education of its people as it has to do with its national defence. If the State is the fountain of all rights, on that principle I would say that it is the source of all duties, and it is the duty of the Government to make some arrangement with the provinces whereby the teaching profession shall be made one of permanency, whereby an inducement shall be given to men and women to remain in the teaching profession and whereby such remuneration shall be given to teachers that they may be anabled to travel and themselves acquire that education which they have not been able to acquire and can never acquire except by travelling.
I ask you, Sir, if the suggestions made in this House by hon. members do not constitute the proper way of building up a nation? One thing that disgusts me every time I hear it is the question which is often put by a French-Canadian or an English-Canadian whenever there is a disturbance of any consequence in the political, social or economical life of Canada: "Why should we not become part of the United- States?'' In 1775 Franklin offered us that national status, and we refused it -because' we knew what it meant. At the rate we are going now, it would appear that Canada can never be all English, nor yet all French, and if the motive is ever to perpetuate affective, mystical and collective illusions, then let them be French in Quebec and English in Ontario. That is the last resource of our patriots. Let us not forget that both the English and the French lost America through political and religious narrowness. The former withheld freedom from the thirteen colonies; the latter withheld refuge from the Huguenots. To-morrow the Wes-t will predominate. Is it not imperative to solve the problem of the school and to base our educational system on lines essentially

Canadian and religious? We all -want the system to be democratic. Let us take the first step in that direction by making it uniform.
Mr. H. C. HOCKE-N (Toronto West): Mr. Speaker, the very -deep interest that has been Taken in the question of national schools in Western Canada has made it inevitable that the subject should at some time be discussed in this House, and it seems to me that this is the most appropriate time for its discussion.
I learn that in August next there is to take place in the city of Winnipeg the largest educational convention ever held in Canada. -His Excellency the Governor General is to preside, and educationalists will be gathered together from all over the continent of North America. That being the case, it is interesting, as I think it is opportune, that some expressions of opinion should be given in this House upon the principal points that will be raised at that conference.
I compliment the mover of the amendment (Mr. Edwards) upon, the courage that he displays in bringing before the House a question of this kind. I knew before he started that he would be charged with bigotry and intolerance. I do not think that he was animated by any such sentiment as that; I -am quite certain that I am not when, following in his footsteps, I advocate the establishment in this country as soon as possible of a national nonsectarian school system.
We are indebted to the member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) for information and quotations which show that the member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) was in good company in bringing this question before Parliament. The member for Maisonneuve told us that the most outstanding advocate of non-sectarian schools in Canada was the late Hon. George Brown, the man who founded the party which hon. gentlemen opposite represent, the man who in the early days made a great fight for Liberal principles. Every Liberal since Hon. George Brown's time who has lead the party represented on -the other side of the House has been his follower. He was an out-and-out, convinced and vigorous opponent of separate schools, and the attitude that he took in hi-s day is practically the attitude that is taken to-day by the member for Frontenac on the floor of this House. He argued then, as we argue now, that two sets of schools tend to disunion and disintegration rather than to national unity, and mutual understanding. The

member for Maisonneuve stated the case exactly when he told us that the late Hon. George Brown accepted forcibly the principle of separate schools being drafted into our Act of Confederation. It was not because. he was brought to believe that it was the right thing to do; he found it to be impossible to effect the Confederation without making this concession to the advocates of the dual school system. He was disposed to sink the lesser in the greater. That is the explanation of his acceptance of the principle of a dual school system of the two provinces of Canada. But the separate schools and the separate school law that we have in Ontario to-day are very different from the statute which was assented to by the late Hon. George Brown. His biographer has told us that when he returned from Ottawa to his home city and was criticised for surrendering his views on the school question, he stated that what had been conceded was innocuous and that, in his judgment, the concession was so small that it could never be profitably worked. I do not know whether he was right or not, but I am inclined to think he was. But this is what happened: No sooner was that particular concession made than the advocates of separate schools proceeded to work on the provincial government and particularly upon the then Prime Minister, the late Sir Oliver Mowat, and during nearly the whole term of his premiership which lasted about thirty years, one concession after another was given to separate schools until, although that is a special privilege to one sect in Ontario, the schools, which they desired and which had been given to them as a special privilege, are almost on a parity with the public school system. That never was in the mind of the late hon. George Brown, because he believed, as my hon. friend said, that what was adopted in 1867, and which was practically the law of 1863, was to be a final settlement. But it is stated in Mr. Hodgins' book upon the Separate School Act of Ontario, in which he quotes all the correspondence of the late Edgerton Ryerson, that while Bishop Charbonnell and Bishop Macdonald agreed that this should be a final settlement, the ink was scarcely dry on the Act of 1863 before additional concessions were demanded. The story that is told in that book is a very interesting one. The writer, Dr. Edgerton Ryerson tells this story that he had a conference with the two bishops and he put this question to them: Is this to be a final settlement of the separate school question in
Ontario? Neither of the bishops said a word, but both of them bowed their assent to his proposition, and he accepted that as a statement from them that it was to be a final settlement. As I say, it was only a few months afterwards before those same ecclesiastics were back in the city of Ottawa demanding further extensions of the separate school principle. This is laid down very clearly in Mr. Hodgins' book.
I wish to correct the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) on another point. In the course of his address to-day, he stated that Separate schools were adopted by the United Parliament of Upper and Lower Canada, with the consent of a majority given by the representatives of Ontario. That was not the case. There was an understanding in the Parliament of the United Canadas that no question affecting one province should be made into law unless there was a majority from that province favourable to it. That undertaking was observed on the part of the representatives of Ontario with the utmost faithfulness, but it was departed from on the part of the representatives of Quebec when the late Hon. R. W. Scott introduced his Separate School Act, and when it came to a vote on that question, it will be found recorded that the vote from Ontario was 26 against and 10 for, with a solid delegation lacking one from Quebec supporting the 10 who voted in favour of Separate schools for Ontario. Therefore, the Separate school system was forced upon Ontario against the will of the majority of its representatives and by a solid phalanx from Quebec.
I think every true Canadian will approach this question of national schools with the desire to see all classes of the population living in harmony and co-operating to realize the great potentialities of our country. As I understand the situation in Canada, it is only by educating our children to be Canadians and by introducing a system that will develop their initiative and cultivate their native talents that we can hope to create a citizenship equal to the great tasks that lie before us. National unity is something that we all profess to regard as essential to our progress, prosperity and happiness as a people. To bring this about, we must understand each other. This does not involve a surrender of our cherished convictions, but it requires an effort on our part to find a way of getting closer together than we are to-day and one that will lead our children to higher levels of service where they may be able to work more harmoniously while main-

24.34

coming together on the football or the baseball field, they show intolerance one of another, and that is directly attributable to the instruction that goes out from these separate schools.
I have a very striking quotation here which I would like to read to the House, because it seems to me to indicate, not only as I interpret it but as an important and influential newspaper of my own province interprets it, that this condition is the result of the teaching in the separate schools of Ontario. I quote from the Christian Guardian, published in Toronto. The writer begins by saying:
Do Roman Catholics feel tlhe same loyalty to the state that Protestants do? Without hesitation we would answer that some of them do; hut it is certain that some of them do not, and this is explained in a recent issue of the Catholic Record.
The Catholic Record, of London, is, in my judgment, the most ably edited and the best-written Roman Catholic paper published in the Dominion of Canada. The men who conduct that weekly newspaper are capable journalists, and theirs is the most creditable journalistic representative of the cause for which it speaks. The article in the Christian Guardian goes on to quote this paragraph from the Record:
We cannot understand the abnormal enthusiasm that the sight of the flag evokes among our intelligent non-Oatholic fellow citizens. They are an enigma to us, and we perhaps are just as much of an enigma to them. Their enthusiastic display of loyalty seems to us puerile and even idiotic. This is because we do not realize that there is nothing that holds a higher place in the affections of the majorit'7 of our non-Catholic Britishers than the flag. In a word, their mentality is different from ours because, if we may use the expression, our household gods are not theirs.
This paper represents the advocates of separate schools in the province of Ontario, and declares in cold type, and after deliberation, that the enthusiasm of the Englishspeaking Protestants of Ontario for the flag is "puerile and even idiotic." I submit that it must be clear to this House that'if we have a system of schools in Ontario that turns out graduates who regard enthusiasm for the flag of the country as puerile and idiotic there is something wrong with the system, and the sooner it is corrected the better it will be for the cause of national unity. I can see no reason why the children of Canada cannot receive their secular instruction together and their religious teaching separately. That is the way the Hebrews in Toronto inculcate their religion. Special classes are held by the

Rabbis, or their assistants, after the regular school hours, and the Jewish children attend for instruction in religion. There is no reason why that plan should not be followed tiiy the Anglicans, Methodists, Presbyterians, and all other denominations. Then we would have a guarantee that the hours in school would be devoted to preparing the next generation for the secular duties of citizenship. If the churches as a whole would undertake the religious education, I am sure the results to the children would be better than those obtained by mixing secular and sacred as at the present time.
What must impress the members of this House as a significant circumstance is the fact that the question of establishing a national school system was first introduced by a representative from the province of Quebec. He introduced this question into the Senate. That his resolution represents the views of a considerable minority in that province seems to be established by several incidents that have transpired during the past year. The province of Quebec for reasons that are within the knowledge of hon. members, is perhaps the last place in Canada from which we might expect such n proposal to emanate. And yet a vigorous propaganda is being carried on there for educational reform. Not much has been accomplished as yet hut experience and history teach us that once a question of this kind is presented by earnest men it gains in strength with great rapidity. Already some concessions, such as uniform text books, have been secured and a compulsory attendance law is bound to follow before long because it has proved to be a wise measure in every country where it has been tried. When it is advocated by men like Lord Shaughnessy and Senator Dandurand and scores of the most prominent lay leaders in the province, it cannot be long resisted. The opposition given to the agitation made by Mr. Bouchard, of St. Hyacinthe, has had the effect of making most of the people do some thinking on that important question. As a consequence of the study given to it we find the Trades and Labour Council of Montreal-two-thirds of the members being French Canadians-passing a resolution in favour of a national school system. These men constitute ithe parliament of labour in the largest industrial centre of the Dominion. They speak for the workers, whose children are the ones most vitally affected by any inefficiency of the school system.

They are men who have come up through the existing schools. They know by personal experience the shortcomings of the schools and with deliberation and earnestness they discuss this question, and by advocating a national school system condemn that which is in vogue. If there is any class of citizens whose voices should be heard with respect on an issue of this kind it is that class who must depend upon the state schools to educate their children.
But it is not only the working classes that are dissatisfied. When men like Mr. nouchard, Senator Beaubien, and many other French Canadian leadens, feel constrained to utter their protest against the inefficiency of the system it becomes apparent that the public sentiment in favour of the motion is widespread and that it includes many different circles.
The press of the province as a whole gives no support to the demand for national schools. Perhaps it is too much to expect that at this stage of the movement. The influences against it are too powerful and apt to resent any attempt to press it forward. Still, ithere are some papers published in Quebec which speak for the movement and do so with the greatest frankness. Among these is L'Autorite, of Montreal, which in September, 1918. said:
Give us less of the stories of Jonah inside or outside the whale, and more of arithmetic. We will even go farther than that and ask that the control of education be transferred from the provincial to the federal domain. Nothing, in fact, is more logical than this, for the reason that where the greatness and the unity of our country are concerned we should have national schools.
That is not the only paper which talks in that way. I have also a clipping from Le Pays, of Montreal, which in an issue of March of this year, declared:
If the men of age to carry arms had been raised in national schools the voluntary recruitment would have given much better results and this province would have received more benefit, for the reason that it was Quebec which suffered most in her reputation.
While I do not offer the opinions of these papers as an expression of the general sentiment of the people of Quebec, they represent a minority which, in my judgment, are thinking along right lines and furthering a movement which meets with the sympathy of the majority in every one of the other provinces.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I am going to try and demonstrate the necessity for some Federal supervision or action, to such limited degree as may be thought wise in connection with their educational system. I submit

that it is well within the province of this Parliament, and of the Dominion authorities, to see that a national sentiment of the right kind is created in Canada. In this connection I want to enlighten the House as to the kind of school books that are being used in the English-speaking public schools of Quebec, which books, I may say, I have examined personally. I find that in the third reader there are three lessons which are complimentary to Britain, and six lessons which are laudatory of Germany; and that book, Mr. Speaker, was reprinted in the year 19X7, three years after the war had started. If that is the kind of stuff that is being taught in schools anywhere in this Dominion, I *think it is only right and proper for the Federal power to endeavour to rectify it. In another reader used in the same class of schools I find the same thing to exist: Two of the lessons are favourable to Britain, and seven are complimentary to Germany. If this had happened ten or fifteen years ago, when we had a different idea of Germany from that which we entertain today, one might not have been surprised; but when such books as these are reprinted in the year 1917, there must be exceeding carelessness somewhere on the part of the authorities, and I submit, some effort should be made to rectify the condition. Certainly a national sentiment, whether it be French or British, cannot be developed by teaching lessons of such a nature.
Now I desire to refer for a moment to the textbooks that are used in the French schools of Quebec. A careful examination of these discloses nothing at all in their contents that would teach a child that it is going to grow up to be a British citizen;
' the sentiment inculcated throughout is purely French. I have no objection to the school books in the province of Quebec favouring the very romantic and interesting features of the early French discoveries and developments; I have no objection to the maintenance of French sentiment in Quebec; but I do say that at the very least there should be lessons in those books such as would teach the children of that province that they are British and are destined to take a part in the government of a British dominion when they attain to manhood. Although I have had a good deal of the contents of these books translated, I will not detain the House by reading at any great length, but I find within their covers such paragraphs as these:
When the United States threw off the yoke England was taught at last that her interests
There is not one school in the whole of the province of Quebec in which the history of the pioneers of Canada is not taught.
I quite believe that that particular side of our history is taught in the province of Quebec, but I wonder if the other side of our history has been taught.

Another side of our history which is also taught in the schools of Que-

That is an old tradition that does not rest on a very stable foundation. I am prepared to agree that the bishops kept Canada from joining in the revolution, but they did it as a bargain, and they got their price. If the hon. gentleman would have us understand that they did that out of pure love of the mother country, he is absolutely and entirely mistaken. They did it because they used that opportunity to get concessions for their hierarchy and for their institutions that they never could have got otherwise.
Is that the kind of history that the hon. gentleman would advocate iiv the uniform books which he would circulate in our schools? If it is, we are sufficiently enlightened.

I would not put that into them; a highly controversial point of that kind might well be left out of any history. But there are many other things about the development of British power in this country that the people of Quebec do not understand, because they have never learned about them. Due prominence and due space is given to that portion of history upon which the people of that province place so much stress; due prominence should be given also to the development of British power in this country. or five grades of the public schools study French, and some of them become quite proficient in that language-at least sufficiently so to pass somewhat difficulty examinations, both in the high school and in the colleges and universities. But after they do learn the language they have no opportunity of keeping it up in our province. My friends of the French race on the other side have ample opportunity of keeping up their English; they speak French in their homes and English in their business.

There is nothing to get excited about. I am trying to explain that there are men sitting all around me who have taken exhaustive courses in French and who cannot follow a French debate today, for the very reason that I have stated. If my hon. friends were in the same position with regard to the English language as we are with regard to the French, they would not know English any better than we know French. But I do not see why -we could not have books of history that would give due place and prominence to all phases of Canadian history; I do not see why we should not have readers containing stories that would tend to develop our British citizenship. I am not entirely satisfied with the school books used in Ontario. I do not think the province has done enough in this connection. I should like to pay tribute to a brother of the member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes), Dr. James L. Hughes, who during the time that he was Chief Inspector of Schools for Toronto, taught patriotism in the schools of that city. One of the reasons why there was such a remarkable recruitment in Toronto was because of the work that had been done 'by Dr. Hughes over a period of twenty years.
Forty years.

There is a collegiate institute in Toronto, round the corner from where I live. I took the trouble to ask the principal of that institute last Sunday night how many of his boys went overseas. Five hundred boys went to the front from that school. The bodies of sixty-eight lie in

France. This collegiate institute is presided over by Col. Hagarty, one of the good loyalists of our city. All these boys went through the public schools of our city and came under the hands of Chief Inspector Dr. James L. Hughes; and if the school books had done their part as well as the inspector did his, there would be nothing to complain of in Ontario.
I believe that this Government intends to give some assistance to technical education. That is a side of education that might be gone into much more thoroughly than it has yet been gone into by the Government. Toronto spent over $2,000,000 on a technical school, and it has not received a cent by way of assistance from this Government or from the Provincial Government. It should have had assistance from this Government; any city should which puts up a high-class technical institution for the perfection of the trades and industries of the country. That is a phase of the work of the proposed Bureau of Education that, I think, would be very valuable.
I have another suggestion to make. The Government, under the direction of such a Bureau of Education as I have briefly mentioned, might appropriate a million dollars a year for scholarships to be given to children, not in the high schools, but in the primary schools. Two or three thousand of these children-those "who win the scholarships-could be taken every year on a two-months' trip over the country. If you took two hundred children from the province of Quebec on a trip through Ontario and the Prairie Provinces to the Pacific coast and back, they would return much better fitted to go on with their studies than they were before they started on the journey.
They would know a good deal more about Ontario and the western provinces than they ever will without isome such visit, and to have them visit those provinces in that way involves an expenditure which the parents are in most cases unable to meet. I would take the Ontario children and send them to Quebec, to the Maritime Provinces, to western Canada, and so I would take the children of every province in this country and send them out through other provinces, at the rate of two or three thousand every year. Thus in the course of ten or fifteen years we would be getting to the point when it would not be easy to say that one province did not understand another. We often hear the statement made that the people of Ontario do not understand Quebec. I fancy that the people of
Ontario understand Quebec a great deal better than the people of Quebec understand Ontario.
We tried something of that kind with grown up citizens in the Bon Entente movement, and it resulted in the Unionist Publicity Committee and the Citizens' Publicity Committee in Toronto.
That was a political dodge.

I am satisfied, as I said last session, that the French Canadian is potentially as fine a citizen as we have. Now, Mr. Speaker, I submit that in a democracy such as Canada a liberal educa-

tion should be placed within the reach of every ambitious boy and girl. The stability of our institutions depends upon the literacy of our people. They rule the country. The Government will be such as they make it. Therefore, it is of the highest importance that every one shouiu receive an education. An illiterate population is the greatest danger to democracy. Unless the people who by their ballots determine the kind of Government we are to have are able to read and write, unless they have their reasoning powers developed by education, they become an easy prey for demagogues and designing manipulators. They must be able to read in order to form their own judgments upon public questions and the more thorough their training is the better qualified will they be to perform their duties as citizens. We have been endowed by Providence with marvellous material resources. It is ours to cultivate the mentality of the common people, to make them ambitious and enterprising by setting before them a high purpose and a goal worth striving to attain. When the Department of Immigration and Colonization was created in, I think, October, 1917, Mr. Cory, the Deputy Minister of the Interior, was appointed acting deputy of the new department. When the Estimates were brought down for the year 1918-19 a vote of $5,000 was taken for a deputy minister, but he has never been appointed. I am sure the Committee will realize the position we were in so far as immigration was concerned during the past year, and instead of appointing a new deputy for the department,
I thought it as well to continue Mr. Cory as acting deputy, and he has consequently acted in that capacity from October, 1917, down to the end of the last fiscal year, and is still so acting.
It is to put him on a footing of equality with the other deputy ministers, I suppose?
No, because during that period other deputy ministers were receiving only $5,000.
But this year they receive $6,000.

Yes. While the department was not active last year in so far as actual immigration was concerned, we have done a great deal of work in reorganizing the department, particularly in Canada and the United States. The entire service in Canada has been reorganized, and Mr. Cory has given a great deal of his time and attention to the work that has been done during the past year. When the Main Estimates of the department are before the Committee, I shall be able to give a fuller explanation of what has actually been done the way of reorganization. I thought it but fair that as Mr. Cory had been appointed acting deputy and has given a great deal of his time and attention to the department during the year he should receive some remuneration for it.

The gentleman referred to is a most excellent officer, and if I make any reference to this item it is simply because of the principle involved, and not because I have any objection to Mr. Cory. He is a deputy minister. Other deputy ministers last year with one or two exceptions, received $5,000. Is it contemplated by this item to pay Mr. Cory $6,000 for the last year?
Yes.

The principle of paying a deputy minister for extra work is a bad principle, and I would certainly ask the
minister to consider it very carefully. A deputy minister is supposed to give all his time to the service of the country, and if he gives a portion of his time from one department to another, is that a reason why he should be paid extra? I have acted as minister for a dozen departments at different times, and every one of the ministers on the front benches to-day is acting for some other department, but are they to be paid an extra salary because they are acting in the absence of somebody else? I think the principle involved is a bad and dangerous one. I have no objection to any salary that may be given to Mr. Cory as a deputy. I am very glad that the deputy ministers are to receive a salary of $6,000; that has my support. But the idea of paying any official in the public service for extra duties is to me a bad and dangerous principle. I think the example of this case will lead the minister into trouble. I repeat, I have no objection to Mr. Cory. He is an excellent officer and I should be glad to see him get the best terms given to deputies of equal rank; it is the principle I object to.

I quite agree with what,
my hon. friend has said as to the principle involved. It is one that should be used with very great discretion. Under the circumstances in this particular case I submit to the Committee that there is justification for the vote. I hesitated a good deal for the very reason advanced by the hon. member, to suggest to the Government that this sum should be placed in the Estimates, but the position was briefly this:	Had I taken advantage of the vote
of $5,000 that was passed in the Estimates last year for a deputy minister, and appointed a deputy, I suppose there would not be the slightest objection at all. Instead of doing that, I have tried to save money for the country. I hoped to save by this method some $4,000. It is quite true that the services of any official of any department should be available when required, but under the circumstances that existed I do not think it would be fair to ask a deputy who has his own work to do, and who should have some time at his disposal to come to my department and my house night after night and spend hours and hours upon work that really was not his own. Now, because I did not take advantage of the vote passed last year, but thought it advisable under the circumstances to try and save $4,000. I am severely criticised. I quite agree that the principle is one which should be safe-

guarded in every way, but at the same time occasions may arise where the circumstances would justify the Government in doing just what it is proposed to do in this case.
iMr. -FIELDING: I think that in the case of minor officials who are receiving but small salaries, allowance should be made for circumstances under which something additional may be paid to them, but even in that case I would rather have it in the shape of a direct plain vote for the salary. There are many illustrations we may have to give as the Estimates come up, because Of think the principle of paying a man in two or three different places is a bad one. I lay down the principle, and I think the minister will agree with me, that the man who receives $4,000 or $5,000, which is a fair salary, not too large-I am not advocating small salaries-owes his whole time to the public service, and any time he may give to the public service is time for which he has already been paid, and he is not entitled to extra pay for such extra work.

Does the hon. member
think for a moment that this official is obliged to go to the minister's house night after night and work for hours without receiving anything extra?

With the statement made that the time of every officer of the Government should be at the disposal of the Government, I quite agree, but it does not appear to me as fair that you should take a man who happens to be in another department and call upon him to give a great deal of his time to work that does not belong to the department of which he is in charge.

No.
