That is right.
I consider Mr. Cory should have $5,000 instead of $1,000.

I understand that the minister is proposing that his deputy should have an increase of salary. If you have a good staff of men who are reliable, trustworthy, honest and industrious, it is poor policy to underpay them. I think this Government are possibly spending a good deal of money in dther directions that might well be spent in paying the employees good, fair, liberal salaries. If the minister of a department comes to this House and makes a statement to the effect, as the minister has done, that he has a good, reliable, trustworthy man on his staff, a man who has been doing not only his own work but the work of another department, and he asks for some compensation for that man, I think we should trust the minister sufficiently to accept this statement and grant the request.

I want to be perfectly frank with the Committee. This is not a question of increasing salaries. The point raised by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens is a very important one. I had a good deal of hesitation in doing this on account of the precedent that is likely to be established and which will probably give the Government trouble in other directions. But it seems to me, taking all the circumstances into consideration, that we will not be establishing a troublesome precedent in this case. I had a good deal of hesitation in suggesting this should be done but at the same time I think it is only fair it should be done.
Who is the deputy minister of Immigration?

Mr. Cory is still acting. I have nobody in sight at the present time but somebody will be appointed shortly.

Department of Railways and Canals, Salaries -$2,250.
Has the Civil Service Commission passed on each of these appointments?

Yes. What happened was this: We have a Purchasing Branch under Mr. Lavoie. A number of the men who belong to that staff and who were employed in the Outside Service have gone to Toronto. Those that are left belong to the Canals Branch and will be paid out of the vote for canals.
Department of Customs and Inland Revenue [DOT]-To provide for a clerkship in the First Division, Subdivision B, Private Secretary-$2,100.
Who is the private secretary referred to here?

The private secretary to Mr. Sifton, Minister of Customs, who is overseas with his chief at the present time.
Post Office Department-Contingencies, clerical and other assistance, further amount required-$10,(MM).
We would like an explanation of this item.
The vote is required to pay certain temporary employees who were engaged to take the places of civil servants who had enlisted and were serving overseas.
Are the temporary employees who are engaged during the rush season appointed by the Civil Service Commission?
The appointments are all passed upon by the Civil Service Commission.
What amount appears in the regular Estimates with respect to this item?

I have not that information. That refers to last year's vote, and this |s a special appropriation to cover the pay of twenty-three temporary employees who were brought in to take the places of employees who had enlisted and gone overseas.
Is this amount intended to supplement the salaries of the twenty-three temporary employees?

No, these persons have not been employed for the whole of the war period. As various permanent employees enlisted, or were called up under the Military Service Act, other men were engaged to take their places and the vote asked for here covers various periods during the year.
[iM>r. Calder.]

I received a letter some time ago from a captain attached to the Canadian forces now in Germany, who belongs to an outside branch of the Post Office Department. He has received his salary and military pay, but desires to know if the bonus granted to the civil servants in Canada will apply to those serving overseas as well?

No, he will not get the bonus.
Civil Service Commission-to provide for the* promotion of one clerk, and contingencies, $20,225.

When a vacancy occurs, in a country post office is it necessary that the Civil Service Commission should advertise and send out circulars inviting candidates to compete for the poorly-paid position of postmaster?
I would not think so.

What is the practice in that regard? I have received circulars drawing my attention, for example, to the fact that there is a vacancy in a post office in British Columbia, or that an engineer is to be appointed in a certain province at a salary of *1,000 or $2,000. I have no interest in such appointments, and it seems to me that those circulars should be sent only to the district affected, thus avoiding a waste of money.

I think my hon. friend's remarks are quite proper in so far as a certain, class of positions is concerned, such as in the Post Office. There is, however, another class of positions which I think should be advertised throughout the whole country.
Technical positions.

Yes. Some discrimination should be exercised, of course. I shall be very glad to call the attention of the Commission to the remarks of my hon. friend.
Legislation-Senate-To provide an amount for the Speaker of the Senate of $3,000 for the fiscal year 1918-19 in lieu of residence and attendants-Further amount required, $1,845.
House of Commons-To provide an amount for the Speaker of the House of Commons of $3,000 for the fiscal year 1918-19 in lieu of residence and attendants-Further amount required, $750.
How much was voted before?
The difference between $1,845 and $3,000.
Is not $3,000 a large amount?
Not when you take into account that the Speaker has to rent a house, engage servants, and so on. He had all that accommodation in the House of Commons.
The Speakers get $4,000 besides their sessional indemnity. I do not see why they should have to rent a house; they could board at a hotel like ordinary members.

Before the destruction of the Parliament Buildings it had always been the custom for the Speaker to have a residence inside the buildings, together with attendants, fuel, and other things. This is merely to replace the loss that he is under on account of living outside.

But I do not see why it should take $3,000 to pay for the rent of a house or of rooms at the hotel. So far as attendance is concerned, I do not see why he needs any. He has a private secretary who is paid by salary. I think there is too much extravagance in that.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

speechtext: It looks to me, Mr. Chairman, as if this were an attempt in an indirect way to increase the salary of the Speaker. I would much prefer that the country pay the actual cost of renting rooms or a house. I understand that the Government is now furnishing a house for the Speaker. ^.Last session I believe he was rooming at a hotel.

The Speaker is paying
rent to the Government for the house he occupies.

But this money was for
last year; it does not cover this year when

he is occupying the house, I understand. If he files a Bill of what he has to pay for rooms I think it would be much more satisfactory than asking for a lump sum, when we do not know whether it is costing that amount or not.

Mr. Chairman, might I
ask if there is a proposal on foot to house the Speaker in the new buildings when they are completed?
No, it is not the intention.

We are departing then
from an old and traditional custom?

Yes.
.General-To pay for Provincial Voters' Lists supplied after the passing of the War Times Election Act, 1917, $7,000.
Explain.
What is that, Mr. Chairman?

Under the law as it stood before 1917 the legal custodians of the voter's lists in the various provinces made up their accounts and sent them to the Clerk in Common Chancery. The WarTimes Election Act, as you will remember, was passed in September of 1917. Most of these lists are made up in the autiynn, and a number of them were forwarded to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery. I believe the contention was that those officials were not acquainted with the fact that it was not necessary to prepare those lists, and after a good deal of consideration a compromise was effected, by which those officials who had actually made up their lists and forwarded them were paid a portion of the amount, and in very many cases the whole.
Those, of course, who had not made them up-a notice was sent out as soon as the clerk found they were coming in-did not receive anything. This $7,000 is required to pay those who actually did send lists in.
The money is paid to some provincial official, I assume?

Under the old law the legal custodian of the voters' list was to make up annually and file with the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery a list as found in his office. The Dominion Government paid that official so much per hundred words for furnishing that list.

There was something more than that. The new Elections Act provided not that the electoral list should be

made, as formerly, by the various secretary-treasurers of the municipalities, sent to the registrar in the county and by that official forwarded to the Clerk of the Crowm in Chancery, but that enumerators should be appointed and Federal lists specially prepared for the purposes of the coming election. The Clerk of the Crowrn in Chancery, probably overlooking the machinery provided by the new Elections Act, sent the usual formal notices to the registrars in the various counties to provide him with the electoral lists as in the ordinary course. That was an error on the part of the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery which is now costing the country $7,000. I agree that the registrars of the various counties should be paid for work that they did at the request of an official of the Crown, but the attention of the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery should be directed to the fact that he made an error which involves an expenditure of $7,000 on the part of the country.

I assure my hon. friend that the fact has been brought to his attention on more than one occasion.
For purchase of seed grains-Governor General's Warrant, Octo<l>er 7, 1918, $3,000,000.
Is this for seed grain for 1919?
Yes.
This seed grain will be distributed now and paid for when it is distributed?
It is sold to the farmers on certain terms-probably the cash is not paid until the crop is harvested.
But the amounts are to be repaid? The Government is not to lose anything?
The Government will not lose anything.
Where is this seed grain distributed?

There was a crop failure last year in several parts of Western Canada, chiefly, I think, in Southern Al-belta and Saskatchewan; and this grain was secured to provide the farmers in those districts with the necessary seed grain.
For purchase of cotton seed meal-Governor General's Warrant, November 19, 1918, $150,000.
Is it the policy of the Government to buy feed and to furnish it to anyone who is short of that commodity, extending to him the credit of the country until the price is paid?

During the latter part of 1918 it was very difficult to secure cotton seed meal and farmers throughout the provinces were very anxious to get it. The Department of Agriculture accordingly purchased cotton seed meal and distributed it among the dealers, and the treasury was recouped.

Last fall it was impossible for the farmers of our part of the country to get hay and grain for their cattle, and they had to sell their stock at a great sacrifice. If the Government was assisting the farmers in other parts of the country, I cannot see why they should not assist the farmers in the Maritime Provinces.

During the war the Government made a great many purchases on behalf of certain of the people of Canada; it was absolutely necessary that they should do so. For instance, all the wool that was imported into Canada during the last year was imported and paid for by the Government, and, through some Governmental agency, distributed to manufacturers in Canada who desired wool. Tinplate was also purchased by the Government and re-sold to dealers-to their advantage, because it was purchased by the Government at a favourable rate. Cotton seed meal was purchased for the same reason. It was practically impossible for private dealers to make the purchases, so *the Department of Agriculture did it, and distributed the cotton seed meal among dealers in the various provinces. The treasury was immediately recouped.
Did any of this cotton seed meal go to the Maritime Provinces?

I think so.
For purchase of stock feed-Governor General's warrant July 2, 1918, $300,000.
What feed is that?

The Government controlled the price of by-products of elevators and flour mills during the war period, particularly during the ' past year. They purchased from the mills bran and shorts, and through some agency or other, they were sold to the public.
What agency?

Some department of Government or some Government agency carried out the details of the work.
Contribution towards the cost of the monument to Louis Hebert at Quebec, $1,000.

In connection with public monuments, may I remind my hon. friend that the Royal Society of Canada last year recommended that a monument be erected in the city of Ottawa to the memory of Edith Cavell, and I understand, that subscriptions have been solicited and a certain amount of money collected. Mr. Benjamin Suite, our well known writer and historian, has taken the lead in the matter and has enlisted the sympathies of many citizens in and around Ottawa. I have been asked by the society, of which I am a member, to request the Government to do its share in connection with the erection of this monument. I hope I shall be able to convey to the Royal Society which meets next week in Ottawa the glad tidings that the Government of Canada will do its share towards the erection of this memorial.
Another point about art-because this item is under the heading of "Arts and Agriculture." I noticed in the Montreal Star last night that two paintings were, amongst others, to be sold at auction in Montreal. As hon. gentlemen are aware, the famous Kreigoff paintings represent Canadian scenery. I have seen a few of those Kreigoff paintings in Senator Edwards' residence in Ottawa and some too in that of the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Murphy). They are very rare and highly appreciated, and I think our museum should have those paintings on its walls. I also noticed in a paper yesterday that the collection of the late Sir George Drummond, containing some of the great masterpieces in the world, was to be sold in London, England. As hon. gentlemen know, there is a law in Italy which prevents any foreigner from taking masterpieces out of Italy to another country. We should have a similar law here. It is known that there are in the residence of at least three or four wealthy Canadians masterpieces of immense value-if they can be valued in money. The collection of the late Sir George Drummond is known not only in Canada but in Europe, and the Art Commission which was appointed some years ago ought not to let this opportunity pass and should see that this collection is retained in Canada for the National museum in Ottawa. I call the attention of the Government to this fact.

I do not think the matter of the Edith Cavell monument has come be-

fore the Government, but it will be taken into consideration.
Pensions-European war-Further amount required, $3,500,000.

The Minister of Militia (Mr. Mewburn) knows that a committee is at present investigating the question of pensions generally, and I suppose he will make a statement to the House some time during the session. Many people are advocating a revision of pensions. I mentioned to the minister the other day some cases of hardship, and I have a promise from him that he will consider the question and later on make a statement to the House.
Major-General MEWBURN: The question of pensions does not come under the Department of Militia and Defence; it is entirely under another department. I am familiar with the cases which the hon. gentleman has mentioned and which I have already referred to the Committee. I have not the privilege of being a member of that Committee. The President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell), who is chairman of the Committee, will, I understand, make a statement to the House.

The statement of the minister is quite correct with regard to the general quesition of pensions, but under the old law, widows of generals were entitled to small pensions, and I think that Act was administered by the Minister of Militia and Defence.
Major-General MEWBURN:	My hon.
friend is quite right. I thought he referred to this item of general pensions.

No.
Major-General MEWBURN: I hope to bring in a Bill amending the Militia Pension Act. There are one or two cases of hardship. I know the case of the widow of a general who served thirty years in the Canadian service, who lost three sons and ene son-in-law in this war, and who lost one son in South Africa. Under those old regulations she draws a pension of only $500 a year. I hope to bring that up on an amendment to the Pension Act.

Another case is that of a widow of a man who served in the Militia Department as general for many years. Since his death she has received a pittance of $500 a year. She has lost her only support in the war, and she naturally expects that the Government will do the fair thing by her.

Just for information, as I was absent last year, I should like to

know the total amount voted to meet the exigencies of the Pension Board in this regard.

The amount voted last year was $15,000,000. This is to meet the excess expenditure for the year. It is due, first of all, to there being a larger number of pensioners that was anticipated when the estimate was originally provided; secondly, to meet the increased allowance for children which was provided during the course of the year, particularly orphan children; thirdly, instead of paying the pensions in advance they are now paid at the end of the month, which means a double payment.
The amount paid last year for pensions was $18,500,000?

Approximately.
Pensions-salaries and contingent expenses of the Board of Pension Commissioners for Canada-further amount required, $500,000.

We understand that the item of pensions must be large, but here is half a million dollars for the salaries and contingent expenses of the board. Is the item correctly worded? It looks a very large amount for salaries and contingent expenses.

It is quite true that the item is a large one, and the explanation is this: The Board of Pension Commissioners, when they presented their estimate to the Government of the cost of administering, estimated some $250,000 in excess of what the Government actually allowed. The Government, in the hope of keeping down the expenditure, cut down the estimate which the Board of Pension Commissioners had presented. As the end of the year approached the board reported that not only could they not keep within the appropriation, but for reasons which they explained to the Government it was necessary that they should exceed even their own estimate by the sum of $250,000. This additional sum was required principally, as I recall it now, for three reasons: First, the working out of their organization in administering the pensions throughout the country had involved a substantial increase in their staff over what they estimated a year ago; secondly, owing to the conditions which prevailed, they have had to pay larger salaries in many cases than they contemplated a year ago; and, thirdly, the expenses incidental to the office and management here in Ottawa at headquarters and at the various centres throughout the country where the board has its branches in each military district have also increased.
Taking this $500,000 and the former estimate, what will be the expenditure on salaries and contingent expenses?
A total of $1,250,000, the former appropriation being. I think, $750,000.

I am not complaining.
I take for granted that there is an explanation. But what is the organization of the Board of Pension 'Commissioners which involves an expenditure of $1,250,000 on salaries and contingent expenses? I am not objecting to the amount, but simply-asking for information. The amount seems very large.

The amount does seem large, and that was the reason the Government a year ago cut down the estimate.
I have not the details here, as I did not expect the item would be up, but when the main estimate is before the Committee I will have full details as to the numbers employed and expenses.
Has the resignation of Commander Ross been accepted?
Yes.
Who succeeds him?

No appointment has been made yet.
Department of Militia and Defence-gratuities, $7,950.39.

Will the minister explain what these gratuities are for?
Major-General MEWBURN: I have the particulars of each one. William Taylor served for 13 years and 13 days as caretaker at headquarters in military district No. 2 at $1.50 per diem. The basis on which the gratuity is calculated is one year's pay for each twenty years of service. N. Ville-neuve was caretaker at the Quebec drill hall for 22 years and 124 days. All these gratuities are calculated on the same basis*
Railways and Canals-chargeable to capital -Quebec and iSaguenay Railway-construction -further amount required, $250,000.
(Mr. J. D. REID:	The work is nearly
completed. This balance is required to carry on the work until the end of the fiscal year.

Gan my hon. friend
state positively when the trains will run into Murray Bay?

The chief engineer
assures me that the regular passenger trains
will be running into Murray Bay not later than the first of July. The work trains will be going into Murray Bay before that, and you could get into Murray Bay on them about the middle of June.
Will there be a daily service?
Yes, after the first of July, during the season.

There is in the county of Charlevoix, along the line of this railway near St. Urbain, a great deposit of a certain kind of iron or ore which was largely used during the war by the General Electric Company of the United States in the manufacturing of war material. I know this company owns a mine there. There is also another company interested in these deposits known as the American 'Titanic Ore Company. The name is American, but the capital stock is owned by Canadian people in Quebec and other parts of the province. This company owns a big mine, but they are unable to operate it at present. During the war they did not have working capital enough. The ore has to be hauled by wagon and horses from St. Urbain to Baie St. Paul, and the haul is too expensive. I noticed one day near Baie St. Paul as many as ten or fifteen cars of ore that had been taken from the mine, and it cost five or six dollars a load. The General Electric Company of the United States are able to exploit their mine, because they h^e a large amount of capital available. I was asked by the people who are interested in this Canadian enterprise to see if it would not be possible, now that the railway is operating to Baie St. Paul, to have a branch line constructed to the mine from Baie St. Paul. This would not only open up the mine, but would give employment to the people of the county, and would alsc facilitate the transportation of farm products. The distance would bo about nine miles. There is also in the county of Charlevoix near St. Urbain, but in another direction, the National Park which belongs to the province of Quebec. Here the Provincial Government keeps magnificent herds of moose and caribou, and other wild animals.
I have no brief for the provincial government but I invite the minister to come down to that part of the country and make one of a shooting party. It would be in the interest of the country if a branch line were constructed there as soon as possible. Would the minister be able to make a statement upon that work?

I give my earnest support to the request made by my hon. friend from Charlevoix (Mr. Casgrain), as I happen .to know that part of the country just as well as I know Ottawa or Montreal. The question of the Saguenay railway has been so many times before the House that I need not repeat the arguments pro and con but the Government has a chance to meet its expenditure in that district by constructing a line to St. Urbain. It is only a matter of 9 miles. There is a large capital invested for the exploitation of that mine, and I am quite sure that if my hon. friend would build a branch line nine miles only in length he would recoup himself for the losses on other sections of the line. This is an industry which ought to be developed. We are very modest in our demands. Whilst my hon^ friend is giving forty-four lines to the people of the West .surely he will not refuse us this little branch line from Baie St. Paul to St. Ur-, bain. My hon. friend has promised me to pay a visit next summer to that district, and I shall make it my duty to accompany him.

I think the hon. member (Mr. Lemieux) will agree that we have about all the railway building on our programme that we can undertake this year. If we complete the Quebec and Saguenay to Murray Bay I think that is about all we can do this year. But I will have the engineer look over the other and make a report.
Will my hon. friend send an engineer there?
I will tell Mr. Grant to have the suggestion looked into and a report made.
Will my hon. friend do that this year?

I will instruct him at once.
Railways and Canals-chargeable to income

miscellaneous-surveys and inspections-railways-further amount required, $10,000.
What survey is that?

This refers to the inspection of railways and surveys. We have men inspecting railways. Different items are paid out of this account. It is an annual vote. Last year we reduced it by $10,000 and then we found that we had to put it in again. Some of the expenses were paid in connection with the investigation of the Canadian Northern railway and

there was a small balance of that which is included in this item.
Labour-Conciliation and1 Labour Act, including publication, printing, binding and distribution of the Labour Gazette, and allowance to correspondence, and for clerical assistance in preparing tables of statistics-further amount required, $10,000. ,
What did the Labour Gazette cost beside the $10,000?

I cannot tell my hon. friend at the moment what the amount was last year. It fell to the Department of Labour during the last year or two to do a great deal more than its ordinary work. There was the Cost of Living Commission which involved the collection and preparation of statistical information.
It did not reduce the cost of living.

It increased the expenditure of the department. That is true also of the vote for industrial disputes investigations; there have been more industrial disputes and consequently additional expenditures have been made.

Disputes in the Government or outside of it?
Administration - Employment Office.-Coordination Act. - Further amount required, $10,000.
Please explain.

Under an Act passed by Parliament, I think at its last session, employment offices have been established in all the provinces, and the work of the Federal and provincial Governments in connection therewith is co-ordinated. Grants have been made by the Federal Government in connection with these offices, I understand.

Parliament passed an Act last session authorizing the creation of labour bureaux in the various provinces. I know there is such a bureau in Montreal, and there are others in the WTest. I would like to get from the minister some statistics concerning the work done by the officers at these bureaux. Have these offices been of real service?
Yes.
Can the minister state approximately the number of men who have been given employment through these bureaux?

The employment offices have done excellent work, and have

been instrumental in securing work for many thousands of persons. I did not expect that the Supplementary Estimates for the Labour Department would be reached this evening, and therefore I am not able to give the data asked for. When the main Estimates of that department are before the House, I shall be in a position to give exact information in connection with this work.

I shall be pleased to have it. because, according to the reports of the meetings of returned soldiers which I read in the press, there is great dissatisfaction among them as regards the operation of these bureaux. The returned soldiers generally say that they have not experienced any satisfaction from them. I do not know whether the statement is true or not, and I would like definite information.
Where is the employment office located in Montreal, and who is in charge of it?

I could not say,
but I will be prepared to give him full information on the main Estimates. I think very probably that the selection of the employment office in Montreal rested with the Provincial Government.

I would like to know
who is in charge of the office, who the staff are, and what salary is paid to each officer?
It is a Provincial Government office, but the Dominion contributes to the cost of administering it.

Would the minister
object to letting the item stand until the information which I have asked for is forthcoming?
There will be opportunity for discussion on the vote in the Main Estimates.

What amount has been
paid to each province under this vote?

The amount
varies. For instance, in the Maritime Provinces I think the Provincial Government pay for the buildings and the furniture and the 'Federal Department of Labour defrays the entire cost of administration. In the case of these provinces the cost of administration is probably not a very large amount.

What amount does Prince Edward Island, for instance, get out of this -mte?
156$

I think it would be a very small sum, but I could not at present give the exact figure. Even if the office in Prince Edward Island has been opened as to which I am not sure, the administration cost to the Federal Government would be very small indeed.
We should have information as to the amount paid to each province. Last year an appropriation of something like $50,000 was made, and now we are confronted by a Supplementary Estimate.-

I do not think my hon. friend was present when the Estimates now under consideration were taken up. These are Supplementary Estimates covering the twelve months up to March 31 last. We are now passing these items so as to get a Bill through and obtain the Royal consent when His Excellency the Governor General attends for that purpose in a day or two. We have not as much information concerning these Estimates to-night as we would have had had we known, that they were coming up, but when the Main Estimates are under consideration the fullest information will be given.

When this item was discussed previously I asked the minister what amount would be apportioned to the different provinces in connection with these employment offices, and I was told that the information would be forthcoming later. Now we have the Supplementary Estimates and still the desired information is lacking. I think the minister who administers the Labour Department ought to be able to tell us how much each province receives.

It was only about the time of the signing of the armistice that the Dominion Government came forward to assist these bureaus which had already been organized and were in operation under the auspices of the Provincial Governments. My impression is that $10,000 is the amount which has been expended upon them up to the close of the last fiscal year. The expenditure for the current fiscal year will, of course, be very much in excess of this vote.
Mr. DuTREMBLAY: The minister states that the amount expended for this purpose since the armistice was signed is only $10,000?

There was an amount voted last year, but after the signing of the armistice the expenditure on this account would increase very rapidly because the problem of unemployment be-

came quite severe about that time. Many new offices were established by the Provincial Governments, and in some instances by the Federal authorities, and last year's vote was found to be short by the amount asked for here.
Mr. DuTEEMBLAY:	I understood that
the Government intended to render substantial assistance to these labour bureaux and that quite a large amount would be needed. If the Government is really in earnest in its desire to co-operate with the provinces in this matter, my opinion is that the sum of $10,000 would only be sufficient to meet the necessities of the office in Montreal.

The amount that will be needed for the current fiscal year will be very much in excess of last year's Expenditure, as the Federal and the Provincial Governments have all been obliged by the necessities of the unemployment prevailing throughout the country to expend considerably more money.

If I am not mistaken a vote of $50,000 was taken last session, and I think no portion of that money, or at least, only a very small amount, was used until the armistice was signed. Then we had a meeting here of representatives from all the provinces, and it was decided to establish these bureaus without delay, either immediately after or immediately prior to the armistice. Since then somewhere in the neighbourhood of seventy-five bureaus have been established. So that the expenditure has been largely since last November.
In all the provinces?

In practically all the provinces. If I am not mistaken the total expenditure will amount, with this $10,000 to something like $60,000. You will find in the Estimates I think for this year a sum of $200,000 to cover the same class of work.
The Minister of Immigration and Colonization last year had this Bill in charge.

No, the Minister of
Labour.

At least, he explained it to me. He explained at that time that it would ease the labour situation, and if I remember rightly, that it was very urgent. I think before we pass this item we should have an explanation of what has been done with the $50,000 and the $10,000.

If we are called upon to vote $10,000 in addition to what was formerly voted, there must have been lots of additional work that was not foreseen. I think we should receive this information.
Soldiers' Land Settlement - 'Salaries of Board of Commissioners-Further amount required, $199.01.
Advances to soldiers settling upon the land, and cost of administering The Soldier .Settlement Act, 1917, including clerical assistance, and amount payable to W. F. O'Connor, K.C., as1 special Counsel to the Board, at the rate of $2,000 per annum, from December 1, 1918- Further amount required, $66'6.66.

This item is a small sinner, but the principle is the same. I have no objection to any liberal salary that may be given to Mr. O'Connor, but I wish to suggest to the minister 'that in the Main or Supplementary Estimates next year Mr. O'Connor's salary whatever it may be, be voted straight and square and not scattered over two or three places.
Who comprises the Board of Commissioners and what are their salaries?
I have not the information here. If the hon. member will let it stand until the Main Estimates are brought down we will give the information then.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?
Let it stand.

I think we ought to have the information. I would like to know where this money is going to, and how many individuals are to receive it. I think it is only fair that the information should be furnished.
